aims: The overall aim of the programme is to enable exploration of the theoretical basis of exercise and sports medicine in general and football in particular, and its application to the development of a physiotherapist's and doctor's clinical reasoning. Using the process of clinical reasoning as its framework, the programme will integrate the key issues central to practice in this specialist area, including: clinical assessment, communication skills, accurate diagnosis, differential diagnosis, diagnostics and prognostics, treatment interventions, management approaches, best evidence, evaluation of outcome, strategies to reduce injury time etc. The programme will facilitate the evaluation of existing evidence through the exploration of the assessment and management of athletes. It will provide students with the opportunity to tailor their learning experience to meet their personal and professional needs, developing their capacity for leadership within an interdisciplinary team providing clinical management in elite sport. The programme will promote enquiry based learning through a range of strategies including case analysis and Problem Based Learning.

aims: This programme aims to provide students with key theoretical knowledge and technical and personal/professional skills that are important for successful practice in high performance sport. It provides an opportunity for students who are interested in careers in sport related occupations to better understand and critically analyse the evidence-based strategies frequently applied to the management and development of athletes and approaches used to ensure successful preparation and competition. It also seeks to consider the application of these concepts to support staff who increasingly impact individual athletes and sports organisations.

In the complex and unpredictable situations that are frequently associated with elite sport there is also a need to identify and develop key personal and professional skills that are associated with individual competence and the leadership and support of others. This programme attempts to deliver active learning experiences for students that span these areas thereby providing a unique opportunity to develop a combination of understanding and competencies simultaneously. The curriculum operates a student-centred problem-based learning approach delivered by a novel blend of experienced academics and practitioners. The implementation of critical friend and peer to peer learning models, along with a diverse real-world self-directed relevant assessment strategy further enriches the educational environment and the opportunity to learn.

Indicative content includes talent management and development, approaches to evaluate performance, key considerations for preparation and competition (nutrition, recovery, training monitoring etc), adaptive leadership, research methods and data analysis, professional practice and independent research skills. The successful completion of this award will provide candidates with important factual, analytical professional and personal skills and experiences that will provide a platform for progression towards employment in high performance sport or similar professional vocations.
The aims of the programme are:
? To enable students to develop knowledge and skills that impact the multi-disciplinary/inter-disciplinary performance of athletes, staff and organisations associated with high performance sport
? To improve student's ability to identify problems, solutions, manage and lead change in response to complex unpredictable situations related to high performance sport
? To develop the critical awareness of important aspects of safe, ethical and effective professional practice
? To support individuals to develop strategies to optimize personal and professional growth in order to maximize the potential to create change in self and others

aims: The programme is designed to produce graduates with integrated engineering knowledge, skills and judgement as broad-based aerospace subject specialists. The programme is distinctive in that:

It provides strong and balanced coverage of aeronautical and space engineering content as part of the core curriculum, ensuring that graduates have a strong foundation for careers in the aerospace industry of the future.
A robust practical element of experimentation and manufacture is maintained to ensure graduates have excellent practical hardware awareness for design and operation of real products and systems.

Modern digital design and analysis tools are fully integrated into teaching and projects, and graduates are equipped with the underlying knowledge and skills to develop and improve these tools as well as simply use them.

Professional and ethical awareness, engineering management, teamworking and leadership skills are delivered with maximum authenticity by fully embedding them into substantive projects; graduates are aware of the impact they can have as champions of areas such as sustainability and inclusive practices and design.
A range of topical, themed optional modules in year 3 and 4 allow students to develop depth of expert technical knowledge, understanding and skills in areas of their interest.

The aims and distinctive features of the programme have been developed via a careful cross-referencing of professional institution requirements, the Engineering Subject Benchmark Statement and the University of Birmingham Graduate Attributes.  The programme is continuously improved, reflecting the professional expectation of any engineering product or service.

The programme is designed so that underpinning scientific and mathematical knowledge and understanding is used as the foundation to develop technical skills in analysis and design through a variety of individual exercises, projects and group activities and projects. Major, capstone individual (BEng and MEng) and group (MEng) projects are both highly synoptic and strongly informed by current research  and/or industry practice and stakeholders. The degree programme makes use of the existing and developing links with the UK / global aerospace industry, which will ensure full topicality of case studies and project topics.

Graduates would be expected to progress to work in areas specific to the degree programme subject areas in the traditional fields of civilian and military aeroengine and airframe design, manufacture and operation along with the materials and sub-systems involved in them. The in-depth coverage of space systems equips graduates for employment in the emerging fields of satellites, space mission and UAVs where remote control and communication is required along with the advanced structures and materials needed for these vehicles and their operating environments. Strong research links in the fields of propulsion and aerospace materials allow progression to research (masters and doctorates) degrees in these fields. Graduates are also well-equipped to pursue careers and research in non-aerospace fields where expertise in advanced materials, manufacturing, structures, aggressive environments and remote communication and control are important. Beyond engineering, numerate problem solvers with strong professional skills are always in demand in a wide variety of careers.

aims: Aim:
To provide postgraduate training to primary care clinicians who are moving from a clinical to a leadership role.
Rationale:
Primary health care is central to health care provision. It is increasingly important as populations in developed and middle-income countries age and develop more chronic conditions.

After clinical training, clinicians (general practitioners, family doctors, pharmacists, allied health professionals) in primary care often take on team leadership roles in primary care organisations. In the UK these might be general practices, or even networks or federations of general practices in the UK. Internationally they might be general practices, primary care clinics or other types of primary care organisations. Health care administrators and managers also often step into leadership roles. While clinicians receive comprehensive training for their clinical roles, there is currently little training available for the transition from front-line clinician to leader.

The programme will teach the principles of leadership and team building in the context of primary health care. It will teach the fundamental principles of the delivery of primary health care, beginning with the underlying philosophy and values of primary care and the characteristics of primary care organisations which deliver care consistent with those values. This includes a patient focus, patient and public engagement in the organisation of primary care, maintaining relational continuity of care and a structured approach to chronic disease management (the chronic disease management model). It also includes the organisational learning system and quality improvement.

The programme will introduce students to epidemiological research and its relevance to primary care. The programme draws on our (IAHR) research expertise and on knowledge of the organisation of UK primary care. The UK has a strong primary health care system and there is international interest in its organisation and implementation.
Skills

Students will develop practical skills in leadership to improve the quality of patient care. They will develop practical skills to create an inclusive team climate which promotes positive attitudes and behaviours.

Students will also develop skills in epidemiological research, an understanding and ability to critically appraise epidemiological studies. They will have the option to develop further relevant research skills through their choice of optional modules.
Work or further study after graduation
Students will most likely take on leadership roles within primary care organisations in the UK or internationally. They may engage in research within a primary care setting.

aims: "The programme aims to develop students? enthusiasm for Earth studies in the broadest sense, to produce graduates with professional skills of observation, critical evaluation, deduction and reporting, and to encourage a habit of maintaining personal competence through study.  Geology and geography have a continuously evolving knowledge base of history and process, rooted in observation of inevitably incomplete and diverse data sets, and given theoretical coherence by an interdisciplinary scientific framework.  In this programme, whose geological content is combined equally with modules provided in Geography & Environmental Sciences, there is a particular focus on Earth's surface processes and environments and the ways these interact with human activities.  The integrated knowledge, understanding and skills acquired fit graduates for careers and/or further study in both geology and geography, particularly in environmental areas, and are appropriate also to a wider field of graduate employment.

The School of Geography, Earth & Environmental Sciences at the University of Birmingham undertakes a wide range of research in the component disciplines, and offers a variety of taught programmes.  The Lapworth Museum, with around half a million geological specimens, is an integral part of the School, and provides a valuable resource for learning and teaching as well as for research.  The Geology & Geography programme provides a broad-based scientific education, integrating material from other major scientific subjects with specifically geological and geographical concepts and skills.  No previous knowledge of geology is assumed.  Fieldwork forms a significant and integral part of the programme, occupying some 30 days.  The structure of the programme ensures that all students are able to develop core knowledge, understanding and skills, but its modular nature allows individuals to develop an academic profile most suited to their particular interests and aptitudes.  Independent project work comprises a major part of the programme, and forms the basis for more than a third of the final BSc classification."

data.progTitle: ForenPsyD  Part-time.
data.shortTitle: Forensic Psychology Pract PT
aims: The University offers a competitive and attractive full-time postgraduate professional Doctorate Programme in Forensic Psychology Practice that combines a number of theoretical and practical approaches and emphasises a developmental and domestic perspective to the study of offending behaviour and criminal activity. It was the first University in the country to offer a Doctorate in Forensic Psychology Practice and has an excellent reputation.

The professional doctorate programme is established as a full time postgraduate course over three years full-time in organised placements or four years part-time for those employed in a forensic setting. The principal objective is to equip trainees in forensic psychology with research and practice skills based on recognised theory and evidence based practice and to offer a sound understanding of criminal behaviour, its effects on victims and appropriate approaches to intervention with both offenders and victims.  Thus, it is aimed at psychologists who intend to work in forensic settings with victims or offenders of crime.   On entry into the Programme, trainees must be eligible to hold Graduate Basis for Chartership (GBC) with the British Psychological Society (BPS) and The Health and Care Professions Council requirements.

Successful course participants will leave the course after three years full time or four years part time with a Doctorate in Forensic Psychology Practice (ForenPsyD) conferring eligibility for BPS Chartered Psychology status and full membership of the Division of Forensic Psychology.  They will also be eligible to apply for registration with the Health and Care Professions Council as a Forensic Psychologist, which is the statutory regulating body for Psychology.

outcome: a) The literature concerning offending and its effect upon victims and a sound understanding of the contribution of psychology to the understanding of criminal behaviour from both a general and developmental perspective (Modules 1 & 4).  b) Client characteristics associated with offending, the ability to evaluate salient aspects of these characteristics together with a similar understanding of characteristics of victims, witnesses, investigators and litigants (Modules 1 & 4).

c) An understanding of the legal and institutional context in which offenders and victims are managed and an awareness of the legal framework of the criminal and civil justice systems, the role of secure units, prison and police services (Modules 3 & 6).  d) A sound grasp of the contribution of psychology to the understanding of criminal justice processes, particularly the process of investigation, prosecution, punishment and treatment. An understanding of the civil processes, for example, non-criminal proceedings under the Children Act.   A familiarity with the contribution of psychology to the understanding of court procedures and decision-making involving the jury process, sentencing and the protection of vulnerable witnesses (Modules 3 & 6).

e) An ability to translate various theoretical approaches to offending and victimisation into practice based interventions and to appreciate the problems associated with turning research into practice.  The work focuses on interventions to reduce offending behaviour and dealing with the needs of both offenders and victims through therapy and counselling (Module 2 & 5).   f) An ability to demonstrate an appreciation of the ethical and professional considerations of evidence based forensic practice and to outline examples of both good and poor practice in forensic settings. The work covers professional issues, the role of professional experts, consultants in intervention and training as well as decision making at local level and policy making at national level (Modules 2 & 5).

g)  To ethically consider a research topic in forensic psychology, critically appraise research knowledge in relation to the topic and to formulate research questions for a secondary research study involving systematic literature review methods (Module 8).

h) The ability to integrate assessment procedures into a coherent formulation of the offending behaviour of individuals, to understand approaches to assessment of individuals, criteria for professional report production and issues relating to consultancy (Module 9, 4).  i) The ability to plan and evaluate intervention, related to formulation and evaluate its progress and to demonstrate a sound understanding of methodology both in terms of the trainee?s own work and in assessing the work of others (Module 9).

j) A sound basic understanding of research methodologies, their practical and theoretical constraints and a sound knowledge of ethical and professional issues relating to good academic research (Module 10).  k) The ability to identify appropriate research questions from the forensic literature, to translate those into scientific hypotheses and to design, plan, implement and report a primary research study (Module 10).
l)  To provide high quality placement reports which identify the core roles performed in relation to at least three different client groups in two forensic settings (Module 7).

m)   To be able to professionally write and reference to publishable standards, to formulate and deliver a) one day training workshop (minimum 4 hours) or b) a conference paper (minimum 15 minutes with questions) training pack and poster, based on presentations derived from the trainee?s forensic psychology primary and secondary research studies (Module 11).

n)   To understand how to develop or modify a psychometric assessment for use in forensic settings and critically assess the psychometric assessment in terms of reliability and validity in comparison to other psychometric and observational measures (Module 12).

o)  To carry out advanced research and evaluation methods based on sound statistical theory.  For example, logistic regression in relation to risk assessment in a forensic population or the development of typologies from cluster analysis and multi-dimensional scaling (Module 10, 13).

p)   The ability to critically assess self-directed research and identify further research questions to build on research work carried out to date, to translate those questions into scientific hypotheses and to design, plan, implement and report on a second primary research study (or expanded study in two parts) of publishable quality (Module 10 + doctoral thesis).

q)  The ability to plan and evaluate interventions related to client needs and to statistically evaluate the outcome of the intervention and assess change in the client resulting from intervention (Module 9).
r)  To provide high quality placement reports that identify the core roles in relation to research and evaluation in a selected forensic setting (Module 7).
learning: a. Formal lectures and workshops from University and honorary University staff.

b. Formal lectures and practical workshops by invited speakers who are experts in their fields. Speakers are encouraged to base their input on the skills training model i.e., description of the skill, practice, research, feedback and discussion.
c. Trainee seminars and case/research presentations.
d. Class assignments, involving active trainee participation, group work and discussion.
e. Computer based learning sessions (particularly for research methods and statistics modules).

f. Individual, one-hour per month, academic tutorials that focus on trainee's input and provide a forum for problem-solving and clarification of complex issues, as well as allowing continual supervision of trainee's progress. Additional group tutorials are also run related to specific assignments (e.g. case studies, court report) and associated experimental design/statistics sections of the course.  An annual review related to trainee progression is also carried out in May of each year.

aims: The degree offers a comprehensive, rigorous introduction to Sociology as a theoretically informed and evidence based discipline. The programme has a strong theoretical core at each level which critically examines the major sociological traditions and perspectives as tools for understanding modern societies. This is paralleled by training in the analysis of empirical sociological research, the design of research programmes and the methods for collecting, interpreting and presenting sociological data. Students are able to apply their core theoretical and empirical training in the critical and comparative analysis of major substantive sociological topics. These include patterns of social divisions such as those of gender, ethnicity and social class. Students approach these issues by pursuing the distinctively sociological questions of the relationships between individuals, groups, institutions and wider social processes; the dynamics of stability and change and the distribution of power. Students complete their degree by designing and undertaking their own substantial piece of sociological research. This brings together their theoretical, methodological and substantive skills and knowledge and is an opportunity to demonstrate the achievement of a skilled, critical and reflexive sociological imagination.

outcome: The character of Sociology as a discipline that is both theoretically informed and evidence based

aims: The aim of the programme is to provide Master's level teaching and research supervision in Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience with a strong focus on Data science. The programme is directed at students with an undergraduate degree in Psychology or Computer Science who wish to increase their understanding of techniques and methods employed by cognitive neuroscience to study the brain using neuroscientific techniques (e.g. fMRI, MEG, EEG), and to develop skills associated with Data science and with proactive problem solving.

Students will acquire skills related to scientific principles and methodologies for a broad range of research. They will acquire in depth understanding of methodologies, and analysis techniques for neuroscientific methods in cognitive neuroscience and computational neuroscience (eg., MRI, EEG, TMS). Students will develop skills associated to data science and proactive problem solving. This may include developing 1) a strong technical expertise in neuroimaging, 2) the ability to prepare data for effective analysis, 3) the ability to write efficient code, and 4) using programs to analyse, process and visualise data.

Although students will experience formal learning in large and small groups, much of the course is focused on informal learning by experiencing research in cognitive and computational neuroscience Students will have opportunities to get to know the more advanced members of lab teams and participate directly in on-going research activity.

aims: The MSc Marketing aims to provide students with a solid foundation in marketing theory and ever-evolving issues in marketing practice. The proposed programme seeks to develop graduates with high standards of knowledge of the principles, theoretical concepts and practice of marketing, giving them the opportunity to choose among digital, international or responsible marketing pathways. The goal is to enable students to develop subject-specific expertise coupled with the critical, analytical, communication and ethical capabilities required for a successful marketing career in today's marketplace.

The core content of the programme provides students with the frameworks, theories and concepts necessary to understand the fundamentals of marketing activity.  Modules will cover marketing strategy, planning and management as well as introducing different perspectives and approaches to the understanding of consumer insights.  They will also be introduced to a range of approaches and techniques to market research.  Students will also be able to explore more specialised elements of marketing activity.  For example, during semester 2 they will study three elements of contemporary marketing practice, namely digital marketing, international marketing, and responsible marketing.

Alongside the knowledge in marketing, students in this programme will benefit from the Birmingham Business School Future Ready Graduate Framework, in which each taught module is supported by academics, careers development and student experience team to develop transferable skills such as agile mind-set, resilience and personal effectiveness. The programme will help students develop the theoretical and practical skills necessary for a successful marketing career. These skills include critical analytical capabilities, problem solving, critiquing literature and evaluating information sources. Further, they will develop their communication skills, both written and oral, and will have many opportunities to practice them by using IT and organising group and teamwork activities.

The programme will be taught in four 4 teaching blocks. Each block is 6 weeks long and there will be two (2) teaching blocks in Semester one (1), followed by another two (2) teaching blocks in Semester two (2). Therefore, in Semester 1A students will have only one core module to attend, and the programme aims to enhance those first 6 weeks with the critical skills for their success in the programme and future career, as per the Birmingham Business School Future Ready Graduate Framework.
Skills development will also be part of the module delivery in semesters 1B, 2A and 2B, but with a lighter workload for students in order to deliver a balanced student experience.

Such a design will allow an immersive learning experience and progression within the programme. Students will enter the programme with limited or no previous marketing experience, while the 6 weeks blocks format will enable them to scaffold to more advanced and specialised knowledge of the discipline and their chosen pathway.  The scaffolding progression enabled by block teaching will allow for four different levels of pre-requisite. In other words, each half semester will form the foundation for the next half.

One of the benefits of this structure is that students also will receive their first end of module feedback quite early in the programme and in their learning journey. The formal feedback in summative assessment from Block 1 will allow a learning opportunity with regards assessment, academic writing, and time management among other benefits. The early assessment and feedback will help students to identify their own strengths and weaknesses. It will also allow programme teams to identify earlier in the academic year areas where extra support is needed in order to tailor the graduate attributes to be developed by each individual student.

aims: This programme combines the study of social anthropology and history.

The social anthropology side of the programme provides students with a comprehensive overview of the discipline of social anthropology, incorporating theoretical and methodological training, and covering a range of topics and sub-fields. Students will gain an understanding of the historical development of the discipline through a syllabus that brings together widely acknowledged anthropological thinkers and schools of thought with critical voices and perspectives. The programme aims to develop an innovative range of transferable skills in research, analysis and presentation, alongside an appreciation of the diversity of contemporary human cultures and societies.

The history side of the programme provides students the opportunity to acquire an understanding of historical events and processes - and of the enduring legacies of the past ? across a range of topics that span diverse chronologies (from the Bronze Age to the present day). geographies and scales (from the West Midlands to Africa, Asia, and the Americas). In so doing, the programme develops a range of analytical and organisational skills, independent and critical thinking, and the ability to synthesise and communicate information and ideas. These attributes will be developed through three interlocked strands of the curriculum:

? Studying History through which students will develop a specialist knowledge of particular historical topics that span a range of periods (from the ancient world to the present day), of geographies (from the local to the global), and themes;
? Understanding History through which students will develop an understanding of the theoretical and methodological development of the discipline and its place in contemporary culture and society;
? and Doing History through which students will undertake original historical research both as an individual and as part of a team.

The programme also attunes students to contemporary challenges within and beyond the discipline - globalisation; sustainability; inequalities ? and to the importance of thinking critically about heritage, conservation, and the place of the past in public life. As such, diversity is the heart of the curriculum. The programme recovers and reintegrates the voices of those previously marginalised by virtue of race, gender, sexuality, (dis)ability, or excluded by virtue of dominant narratives of the past and enables and encourages students to explore the histories and cultures of different peoples, societies, and cultures from around the world. The programme challenges students to engage with communities in the city, the region, and beyond.

Graduates will display a broad knowledge of social anthropology and history and be able to demonstrate intellectual versatility and organisational flexibility. The programme will encourage independent and critical thinking, culminating in a dissertation based on supervised independent research in the final year of study in either social anthropology or history.

The programme will prepare students for a wide range of careers and will provide a sound base for further study in social anthropology, history or related disciplines. Students will develop the transferable skills that are associated with all arts, humanities and social science degree programmes, including: identification of areas of enquiry and relevant sources of information; referencing, evaluation, synthesis and analysis of information in the light of relevant methodological and theoretical frameworks; clear and coherent communication in person and on paper.

aims: This programme combines social anthropology and interdisciplinary African studies.

The social anthropology side of the programme provides students with a comprehensive overview of the discipline of social anthropology, incorporating theoretical and methodological training, and covering a range of topics and sub-fields. Students will gain an understanding of the historical development of the discipline through a syllabus that brings together widely acknowledged anthropological thinkers and schools of thoughts with critical voices and perspectives.

The African Studies side of the programme introduces students to the study of Africa from a range of disciplinary perspectives. Students will study the history, politics and culture of a range of African societies. Drawing on primary sources and scholarly analyses of African societies from the pre-to the post-colonial era, the programme encourages an awareness both of the dynamics of change over time and of the place of sub-Saharan Africa within the global context. By learning through an interdisciplinary lens, students will develop the ability to work with different methodological and analytical frameworks.

Joint Honours graduates will display a broad knowledge of social anthropology and African studies and be able to demonstrate intellectual versatility and organisational flexibility. The programme will encourage independent and critical thinking, culminating in a dissertation based on supervised independent research in the final year of study in either social anthropology or African studies.

The programme will prepare students for a wide range of careers and will provide a sound base for further study in social anthropology, African studies, history, international development or related disciplines. Students will develop an innovative range of skills in research, analysis and presentation, alongside an appreciation of the diversity of contemporary human cultures and societies within and beyond Africa. Graduates will have the transferable skills that are associated with all arts, humanities and social science degree programmes, including: identification of areas of enquiry and relevant sources of information; referencing, evaluation, synthesis and analysis of information in the light of relevant methodological and theoretical frameworks; clear and coherent communication in person and on paper.
For Year/Semester abroad only:

Study abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. Study abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.

aims: BA Drama and Film is characterised by a wide study, which is methodologically- and theoretically- informed, of Film, ranging across genres, modes and media, combined with the theoretical and practical exploration of a wide range of theatrical and performance styles, from British playwrights and actor training to immersive practices and directing.

Students will develop a deep and rich understanding of the generative, compositional and self-reflective processes involved in creative work in both disciplines, learning practical, technical and industry-specific skills en route. Students will also engage critically with the history and thematic dimensions of both disciplines, encountering a wide range of approaches to Drama and Film in different historical periods. In the third year, students will have the opportunity to take the Professional Skills Module, to undertake a placement or progress their own entrepreneurial project.
The programme aims to produce individuals who possess a broad range of knowledge and understanding of Drama and Film. It will give students the opportunity to:
Develop analytical and practical skills derived from close reading of a wide range of film and performance texts and informed by critical studies
Understand different modes of representation on stage and on film, and how they are socially and politically informed
Gain skills in writing, reasoning, presentation, performance and independent research
Work creatively through film and performance practices to explore a diversity of ways of engaging different audiences
Understand the histories and practices of film-making and performance, underpinned by key theoretical approaches
Develop interpersonal and communication skills, with particular strengths in collaboration and teamwork
Gain an understanding of how to narrate these skills to future employers.

The wide range of reasoning, research, independent learning, communication and creative skills acquired from this programme equips graduates to pursue further study or employment in Drama and Film related disciplines, and is readily transferable to a variety of commercial, cultural and professional careers, including the creative arts, film or media sectors.
For semester/year abroad programmes only:

Study abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. Study abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in an unfamiliar setting.
For Year in Civic Leadership only:

The Year in Civic Leadership allows students to put into practice the theoretical knowledge and skills developed during their academic studies, and to critically reflect on this activity, by devising a civic engagement project in collaboration with local community actors. The modules deepen student's appreciation of civic engagement, encouraging them to think about how they can enrich the communities they live and work in.

aims: This programme aims to develop the intellectual, analytical, problem-solving and communication skills of students by providing them with a breadth of knowledge of business management, together with the transferable skills (for example in group and team working) that are necessary to apply this knowledge in new and challenging contexts. The underlying philosophy of the programme is that students study all aspects of business management and whilst they have some flexibility to follow their own interests they do not become overly specialised in one business related theme. However, the programme develops a thorough understanding of Business Management as a broad discipline and develops an appreciation of research relevant to that discipline. In consultations with employers we are told that they value the broad-based knowledge that our graduates  The fact that business is conducted today in a global environment and the necessity to interact with other markets and cultures, means an international underpinning is to be found in most modules. In addition, the programme progresses an understanding of the role of individuals and business in society. It develops effective problem-solving skills and an ability to communicate well using a range of media. The programme recognises the increasing role of business in society and so develops knowledge of ethical issues and practices across the discipline whilst evolving awareness of individual and collective citizenship as a part of responsible business. An appreciation of other contemporary issues such as entrepreneurship and knowledge management is provided throughout the programme.  Year One is a foundation year and therefore is compulsory. In this year all the key themes of the programme, i.e. Organisations and Entrepreneurship, Marketing and Communications, Business Economics, Accounting and Finance, are introduced and students are given a thorough grounding in the subject areas they are to continue in later years.   Year 1 also contains a key skills module for personal and academic development, and a choice of study outside the main discipline, allowing wider interests to be pursued in the foundation year. In Year Two students continue to develop a deeper understanding of responsible business and the relevancy of discipline relevant research. Although still broad based, modules begin to become more focused and specialised within programme themes.  Year Three features modules that are increasingly advanced focused, allowing students more specialisation along with an increased degree of choice, whilst maintaining a relatively broad spectrum across the discipline. The year is underpinned by a compulsory extended project/dissertation (20 credits) which allows the student to investigate in depth an area of personal interest.

aims: This Taught LLM programme enables graduate students, both from within the European Union and elsewhere, to develop expertise in a variety of subjects in which the School of Law has significant strengths. aims: This is an interdisciplinary programme which is focused on developing excellent professional practice in a range of sport-related contexts. Students are engaged in modules that draw from a range of disciplines. A key feature of the programme is its focus on synthesising theory and practice in applied contexts. Areas of study include a wide range of topics on sport pedagogy (teaching and coaching), applied sport sciences (i.e. psychology, physiology, motor control), sport policy and management, and research methods.  Modules across the school provide the opportunity to study in many areas from both scientific and applied perspectives, and there are increasing opportunities for choosing modules in the second and third year of studies. aims: The Masters in Mental Wellbeing at the Dubai campus of University of Birmingham was developed to meet the diverse needs of the growing mental health sector in the UAE.

Clinical knowledge and skill are developed through diverse pedagogical approaches including hybrid content, seminars and flipped classrooms to name a few. Emphasis is placed on the translation of knowledge into practice. Examples of this include developing intervention plans (formulations) from case studies, practicing delivery of interventions in role play scenarios and formative feedback sessions aimed at unpicking the clinical decision making. Knowledge of this competency pillar is underpinned by practical sessions allowing continuous formative feedback to allow for progressive development in preparation for the practical placements in the second year of study.

The master also embeds research training and an independent, mental health research project as part of the compulsory suite of learning and outcomes. This aims to address the significant knowledge, skill, and competency gap within the mental health sector, to enhance research/evidence-based practice and service development. Students will develop the research knowledge and skill to undertake rigorous and culturally sensitive clinical research, evaluate the existing evidence and the translation of research into best clinical practice. This focus on the development of scientific practitioner is imperative to effective service development, policy development, and evidence-based practice, crucially to meeting the growing mental health concern in the region.
Areas of work include government and private mental health support providers, policy development, evaluation, research, and academia.
The specific aims of the Masters are:
1. To develop knowledge and skills in assessment and formulation across diverse mental health conditions and populations
2. Develop the knowledge and skill necessary to delivery CBT and at least one other therapeutic approach
3. Engage in ethical, anti-discriminatory, professional and reflective practice
4. Evaluate the existing research and evidence in mental health and how this translates into best practice and policy
5. Conduct autonomous, original research, that is clinically relevant and culturally sensitive to middle east context.

aims: BA Drama and English Literature is a Single Honours Programme, including study in ancilliary disciplines. It is characterised by a wide study, methodologically and theoretically informed, of the range of literature in the English language from the medieval period to the present, and by the theoretical and practical exploration of a wide range of theatrical and performance styles, from the Renaissance stage to the present. It aims to produce individuals who possess a broad range of knowledge and understanding of English literature and performance; critical skills in the close reading and analysis of texts both literary and non-literary; analytical and practical skills derived from the close analysis of dramatic and performance texts and contexts; organisational and presentational skills, including those derived from work on the production and organisational aspects of theatre and performance; and a developed competence in interpersonal and communicative skills, with particular strengths in collaborative work. The wide range of reasoning, research, independent learning, communication and organisational skills acquired from this programme equips graduates to pursue further study or employment in English, Drama and related disciplines, and is readily transferable to a variety of commercial, cultural and professional careers.
For year abroad only:

Study abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. The year abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.

aims: The MSc Advanced Practice in Healthcare (international)

aims: This Taught postgraduate programme in Midlands and Local History enables students to develop expertise in this sub-discipline of History in which the Department of History has significant strengths. The programme aims to:

1. enable students to acquire a systematic understanding of the history of the Midlands region with a focus on the early modern period to the present, and to gain a critical awareness of current problems and/or new insights, much of which is informed by, or at the forefront of, the studied subject.
2. enable students to acquire a comprehensive understanding of techniques applicable to their own research and advanced scholarship in the history of the Midlands.

3. encourage students to demonstrate originality in the application of knowledge, together with a practical understanding of how established techniques of research and enquiry are used to create and interpret knowledge in the sub-discipline of local history, as well as the wider discipline of history.

4. enable students to acquire a conceptual understanding that allows them to evaluate critically current research and advanced scholarship in the sub-discipline of local history, as well as the wider discipline of history.

5. enable students to develop their skills in research and writing in the sub-discipline of local history through preparing assessed work and a substantial dissertation written under the supervision of a specialist in the subject.

6. enable students to gain a mixture of generic and discipline-specific skills, providing a solid base both for academic research into the history of the Midlands or an allied discipline at doctoral level, and also for the development of a professional career, including (but not limited to) fields adjacent to the historical discipline.

data.progTitle: BA Social Anthropology with African Studies Full-time
data.shortTitle: BA Soc Anthrop w Afr Stu FT
aims: This programme combines social anthropology and interdisciplinary African studies.

The social anthropology side of the programme provides students with a comprehensive overview of the discipline of social anthropology, incorporating theoretical and methodological training, and covering a range of topics and sub-fields. Students will gain an understanding of the historical development of the discipline through a syllabus that brings together widely acknowledged anthropological thinkers and schools of thoughts with critical voices and perspectives.

The African Studies side of the programme introduces students to the study of Africa from a range of disciplinary perspectives. Students will study the history, politics and culture of a range of African societies. Drawing on primary sources and scholarly analyses of African societies from the pre-to the post-colonial era, the programme encourages an awareness both of the dynamics of change over time and of the place of sub-Saharan Africa within the global context. By learning through an interdisciplinary lens, students will develop the ability to work with different methodological and analytical frameworks.

Joint Honours graduates will display a broad knowledge of social anthropology and African studies and be able to demonstrate intellectual versatility and organisational flexibility. The programme will encourage independent and critical thinking, culminating in a dissertation based on supervised independent research in the final year of study in either social anthropology or African studies.

The programme will prepare students for a wide range of careers and will provide a sound base for further study in social anthropology, African studies, history, international development or related disciplines. Students will develop an innovative range of skills in research, analysis and presentation, alongside an appreciation of the diversity of contemporary human cultures and societies within and beyond Africa. Graduates will have the transferable skills that are associated with all arts, humanities and social science degree programmes, including: identification of areas of enquiry and relevant sources of information; referencing, evaluation, synthesis and analysis of information in the light of relevant methodological and theoretical frameworks; clear and coherent communication in person and on paper.
For Year/Semester abroad only:

Study abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. Study abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.

outcome: 1. A range of sub-Saharan African environments and societies, and the dynamics of change over time (CertHE/DipHE/BA)

aims: This programme combines the study of Social Anthropology and Classical Literature and Civilisation.

The Social Anthropology side of the programme provides students with a comprehensive overview of the discipline of Social Anthropology, incorporating theoretical and methodological training, and covering a range of topics and sub-fields. Students will gain an understanding of the historical development of the discipline through a syllabus that brings together widely acknowledged anthropological thinkers and schools of thought with critical voices and perspectives. The programme aims to develop an innovative range of transferable skills in research, analysis and presentation, alongside an appreciation of the diversity of contemporary human cultures and societies.

The Classical Literature and Civilisation side of the programme provides students the opportunity to explore the diversity of Greek and Roman culture, drawing together literature, drama, myth, religion, history, philosophy and art. Students will analyse a wide range of evidence (material, written, digital) to explore the interconnected nature of Greek and Roman societies with each other and other cultures of the Mediterranean and beyond. The programme contributes to students? understanding of the origins of modern culture, enabling students to engage critically with the Classical world and its impact on the modern world.

Graduates will display a broad knowledge of Social Anthropology and Classical Literature and Civilisation and be able to demonstrate intellectual versatility and organisational flexibility. The programme will encourage independent and critical thinking, culminating in a dissertation based on supervised independent research in the final year of study in either social anthropology or Classical Literature and Civilisation.

The programme will prepare students for a wide range of careers and will provide a sound base for further study in Social Anthropology, Classical Literature and Civilisation or related disciplines. Students will develop the transferable skills that are associated with all arts, humanities and social science degree programmes, including: identification of areas of enquiry and relevant sources of information; referencing, evaluation, synthesis and analysis of information in the light of relevant methodological and theoretical frameworks; clear and coherent communication in person and on paper.
For year abroad only:

Study abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. Study abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.

aims: This cross-disciplinary programme equips students to lead responsible innovation of real-world healthcare with AI technologies. It addresses the persistent skills gap in the healthcare workforce which is an internationally acknowledged barrier to AI-enabled healthcare. Leaders in AI-enabled healthcare will come from many backgrounds, with deep expertise in varying domains. Despite this variation, each will require knowledge and skills across a breadth of topics. To align with this need, this programme prioritises accessibility. It is designed to deliver the breadth of competencies required for AI implementation, without demanding deep clinical, operational or technical expertise from any individual applicant. Practically this allows us to welcome recent graduates of biomedical, managerial or technical undergraduate programmes alongside mid-career professionals into our diverse learning community.

Complementary modules will equip students to characterise real-world problems in healthcare and identify quality assured AI health technologies which can effectively target them. Students will then learn principles and techniques which allow them to tailor safe, effective and fair implementation efforts for the various AI technologies and healthcare contexts they may encounter. The curriculum is based on active research to consolidate best practices among trailblazing healthcare provider organisations in the US and UK, and the content will be continually updated to keep pace with this emerging field. This is facilitated by the multidisciplinary and global network in which the programme's faculty are situated, enabling contributions from prominent guest lecturers across the programme.

The MSc programme concludes with a capstone project, grounded in practical AI implementation issues. This is facilitated by the faculty's connection to University Hospitals Birmingham, one of the UK's largest NHS trusts and earliest adopters of AI technologies. This practice-orientated conclusion allows students to bring together the range of skills and knowledge they have acquired and smooth their transition from study to practice. Graduates will emerge ready to lead the implementation of AI into varied healthcare settings, through roles in healthcare providers, MedTech companies, healthcare consultancies or policy.

outcome: 1. Critically analyse healthcare pathways and interventions, identifying key stakeholders and demonstrating effective strategies for their engagement in AI implementation projects (Applicable to the following qualifications: MSc; PGDip)

2. Synthesise evidence and stakeholder perspectives to develop a compelling value proposition for AI innovations in healthcare including measurable outcomes and success criteria (Applicable to the following qualifications: MSc; PGDip)

3. Demonstrate an understanding of the evidence needs of diverse healthcare decision-makers (e.g., clinicians, administrators, policymakers) when implementing AI solutions, drawing on interdisciplinary knowledge to tailor communication strategies (Applicable to the following qualifications: MSc; PGDip)

4. Develop comprehensive monitoring and evaluation plans for AI interventions in healthcare, incorporating metrics to assess patient outcomes, safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness, ensuring sustained benefits and responsible use (Applicable to the following qualifications: MSc; PGDip)

5. Critically analyse the policy landscape, regulatory frameworks (e.g., Medical Device Regulation, ISO standards), and system-level factors influencing AI innovation in healthcare, demonstrating the ability to integrate these considerations into implementation plans. (Applicable to the following qualifications: MSc; PGDip)
6. Be able to demonstrate analytical, reflective and independent thinking and working.  (Applicable to the following qualifications: MSc; PGDip)

aims: The MRes in Biomedical Sciences programme is aimed at life science students who wish to develop research careers in a range of biomedical disciplines. The themes are Cardiovascular Sciences, Inflammation and Aging, Neurogenetics, Immunology and Neuropharmacology.  It is anticipated that over time additional themes will be incorporated into this programme and the clear framework will make this more achievable for new themes.

In the discipline specific module, students will be exposed to research-led teaching by academics in the area - they will be given a fundamental grounding in the subject area as well as learning about the cutting-edge research being undertaken by the academics within that theme.  The core research skills module will give the student a range of essential skills which will underpin their research project, including experimental design, data interpretation and presentation, critical analysis of the literature, statistics, bioinformatics and the introduction to a variety of fundamental techniques. After completing the taught components, students will start their 120 credit research project hosted by a research group aligned to their theme of choice.  Students will be embedded in their research groups for 9 months and this element of the programme is part of the post-graduate research degree pathway.  The culmination of the project will the preparation of thesis that will be examined by experts in their field.  Students will have opportunities to attend conferences to present their work and it is anticipated that their work will contribute to scientific outputs by their host laboratories.   It is expected that this programme will be highly attractive and relevant to students who wish to further their postgraduate studies at PhD level but also to students wishing to pursue alternative scientific career pathways. Thus, the programme will provide students with a strong grounding subject discipline and allow them to become stronger candidates for PhD programmes and other research positions.

aims: Understanding climate and environmental change, how we address its causes, how we live with and respond to its impacts, and how we find sustainable solutions to our use of Earth's resources and impacts of planetary systems, is one of the most pressing issues facing humanity. This one-year programme aims to introduce environmentally motivated students studying in a range of disciplines to the core concepts of environmental change and sustainability, from the perspective of planetary processes and environments impacts, and in terms of developing sustainable solutions to present-day challenges. In an increasingly globalised world, it is of paramount importance that we are able to develop sustainable and interdisciplinary approaches across management of energy, natural resources, food security, biodiversity, ecology, and natural hazards.

Tackling themes across environmental sustainability requires a broad and interdisciplinary approach, and a working knowledge of Earth and Environmental processes and the intersection of human pressures on ecological systems. This one year of study meets this need by providing students with a broad foundation in Earth and Environmental Science and Biosciences, giving the student a working introduction to sustainability challenges alongside a range of transferable cross-disciplinary skills that will support students? skills and careers irrespective of discipline.  The constituent modules introduce the necessary understanding and skills to address the challenges posed by global environmental change and aim to take an interdisciplinary and practical approach.

Graduates who have added this additional year to their existing programme will enter their final year with a different perspective on their core studies and will be equipped for a wider range of graduate employment.

aims: BA English Language and Literature is characterised by a wide study, methodologically and theoretically informed, of the range of literature in the English language from the medieval period to the present, and by study of the structure and character of the English language. It aims to produce individuals who possess a broad range of knowledge and understanding of English literature and performance; critical skills in the close reading and analysis of texts both literary and non-literary; responsiveness to the central role of language in the creation of meaning; rhetorical skills of effective communication and argument, both oral and written; bibliographic skills appropriate to the discipline; understanding of the role of cultural norms in comprehension and judgement; and awareness of how different social and cultural contexts affect the nature of language and meaning. The wide range of reasoning, research, independent learning, communication and organisational skills acquired from this programme equips graduates to pursue further study or employment in English and related disciplines, and is readily transferable to a variety of commercial, cultural and professional careers.

outcome: A substantial number of authors and texts from different periods of literary history

Thematic and generic links between texts across a wide historical range

The structure and character of the English language, including phonology, lexis, grammar and discourse
Analytic practices in the description of the English language and traditions in linguistic theory;
Current methodologies and practices used in linguistic research
The variation of English language in different situational and developmental contexts and the theoretical frameworks within which such variety is studied
The grammar, discourse and lexis of varieties of English and critical and cultural frameworks within which such variation is studied

aims: This Taught LLM programme enables graduate students, both from within the European Union and elsewhere, to develop expertise in a variety of subjects in which the School of Law has significant strengths. This taught LLM programme provides a supportive environment in which students take responsibility for their own learning and aim to become effective life long learners.
The programme aims:

1.  to enable students to acquire a systematic understanding of the subjects they study, and a critical awareness of current problems and/or new insights, much of which is at, or informed by, the forefront of the subjects studied.
2. to enable students to acquire a comprehensive understanding of techniques applicable to their own research and advanced scholarship.

3. to encourage students to demonstrate originality in the application of knowledge, together with a practical understanding of how established techniques of research and enquiry are used to create and interpret knowledge in the discipline.
4. to enable students to acquire a conceptual understanding that allows them to evaluate critically current research and advanced scholarship in the discipline.
5 to enable students to develop their skills in research and writing through preparing assessed work and a substantial dissertation written under the supervision of a specialist in the subject.

outcome: 1. aims: BA Film and Creative Writing is characterised by a wide study, methodologically- and theoretically-informed, of a range of topics of study in Film and Creative Writing, ranging across genres, modes and media. Students will develop a deep and rich understanding of the generative, compositional and self-reflective processes involving creative work in both disciplines, learning practical, technical and industry-specific skills en route. Students will also engage critically with the history and thematic dimensions of both disciplines, encountering a wide range of theoretical approaches to film and creative writing in different historical periods. They will develop critical skills related to writing, reasoning, presentation and independent research through formative and summative assessment on the programme, alongside a sophisticated understanding of how to narrate those skills to future employers. The programme will prepare students for a wide range of careers in the creative arts, filmic or media sectors, and will provide a sound base for further study in any of these disciplines.

For semester/year abroad programmes only:Study abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. The year abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.

aims: The MSc Economics programme is designed to provide an advanced training in Economics, suitable for students who wish to progress into careers as professional economists in the public or private sectors, for example in the Government Economic Service or overseas equivalents, regulatory agencies or economic research institutes. It is also designed as a route onto PhD programmes and research in Economics, as well as a broader range of careers suitable for Economics graduates.

The programme will provide all students with an advanced training in the core areas of micro- and macroeconomics and econometrics, and an opportunity to specialise in more policy-oriented or more quantitative areas. It is aimed at students who have an undergraduate degree in Economics, or with a significant component of Economics and a quantitative focus.

Students completing this MSc degree will acquire the disciplinary knowledge and competence in methodology and techniques required for research and policy analysis in Economics, and generic skills that are applicable across a wide range of careers. They will become acquainted with recent developments in the subject, and will be able to understand and critically assess articles at or near the frontiers of research.

Within the programme, three named specialisms will be available to students who choose 40 optional credits and write a dissertation in the area. These specialisms are in Environmental and Natural Resource Economics; Behavioural and Experimental Economics; and Development Economics. Each of these pathways is designed to prepare students for more specialised policy work or research within the named area.
USP(s) and why students would come to UoB

While recognising that strong theoretical and mathematical foundations are important within the subject, in designing the new programme we also recognise that the economics most graduates will use in their careers is likely to be more applied. In particular, graduates are more likely to apply micro- and macroeconomics in empirical and policy analysis than to need to formally derive mathematical models. They will need to be comfortable using up-to-date techniques and software to analyse data, without necessarily needing to derive the underlying econometric models. However this needs to be balanced with the need to prepare students who wish to move into research and will require strong theoretical and quantitative foundations.
Additionally, by enrolling on this programme, students will benefit from:

1. Being taught by prominent academics with expertise in various areas of economics. Students will gain critical awareness and understanding of the theoretical foundations of economics and its applications.

2. Being trained in advanced analytical skills and research methods. Students will receive comprehensive training in advanced techniques to deal with a wide range of issues in empirical and policy analysis.

3. Exposure to distinctive areas of research strength in the Department, such as behavioural and experimental economics, and environmental and natural resource economics, which will also allow students to focus on issues relating to sustainability.

aims: History:

The History side of the programme provides students the opportunity to acquire an understanding of historical events and processes - and of the enduring legacies of the past ? across a range of topics that span a diverse range of chronologies (from the Bronze Age to the present day) and geographies and scales (from the West Midlands to Africa, Asia, and the Americas). In so doing, the programme develops a range of analytical and organisational skills, independent and critical thinking, and the ability to synthesise and communication information and ideas. These attributes will be developed through three interlocked strands of the curriculum:

? Studying History through which students will develop a specialist knowledge of particular historical topics that span a range of periods (from the ancient world to the present day), of geographies (from the local to the global), and themes;
? Understanding History through which students will develop an understanding of the theoretical and methodological development of the discipline and its place in contemporary culture and society;
? and Doing History through which students will undertake original historical research both as an individual and as part of a team.

The programme also attunes students to contemporary challenges within and beyond the discipline - globalisation; sustainability; inequalities ? to the importance of thinking critically about heritage, conservation, and the place of the past in public life. As such diversity is the heart of the curriculum. The programme recovers and reintegrates the voices of those previously marginalised by virtue of race, gender, sexuality, (dis)ability, or excluded by virtue of dominant narratives of the past and enables and encourages students to explore the histories and cultures of different peoples, societies, and cultures from around the world. The programme challenges students to engage with communities in the city, the region, and beyond.
For year abroad programmes only:

The year abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. The year abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.
English Literature aims:
a wide study, methodologically and theoretically informed, of the range of literature in the English language from the medieval period to the present;

through study of the range, kinds, structure and character of literature in the English language it aims to produce individuals who possess a broad range of knowledge and understanding of English literature and performance;

to instil in students critical skills in the close reading and analysis of texts both literary and non-literary; responsiveness to the central role of language in the creation of meaning; rhetorical skills of effective communication and argument, both oral and written;
to provide students with bibliographic skills appropriate to the discipline;
to provide students with an understanding of the role of cultural norms in understanding and judgement;
to provide students with awareness of how different social and cultural contexts affect the nature of language and meaning.

The wide range of reasoning, research, independent learning, communication and organisational skills acquired from this programme equips graduates to pursue further study or employment in English and related disciplines, and is readily transferable to a wide range of commercial, cultural and professional careers.

aims: To enable students to achieve the appropriate level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (specified by language under Learning Outcomes) through the systematic integration of language and content teaching.
To enable students to explain and assess critically the multi-disciplinary features and significance of the culture, history and society of their chosen language communities.

To enable students to be digitally literate. Students will be able to use appropriate, up-to-date technology in the effective learning of languages and to understand works of culture (understood in the broadest sense, to include history, society, politics, and other material covered in modules aligned with the Birmingham Languages Graduate).
To enable students to handle and analyse material relating to research projects based in the Department of Modern Languages.
*To enable students to engage with appropriately adapted questions derived from research projects based in the Department of Modern Languages.
To enable students to become effective independent learners, with regular opportunities to develop skills in research, academic writing, and reflective learning.

To enable students to be competitively employable through the acquisition of direct and transferable skills as well as through: 1) appropriate integration of Modern Languages careers topics within core modules; 2) optional placement opportunities relating to Modern Languages (credit-bearing and non-credit-bearing); 3) non-credit bearing Modern Languages careers events.
*To enable students to give a persuasive account of their degree and of why they have assembled their degree in a particular way.

To provide students with language and language-related transferable skills useful in a range of contexts, both educational and professional; and to respond to national and international needs for advanced strategic competence in a variety of world languages.
To enable students to acquire first-hand experience of living and studying and/ or working abroad.

To enable students to develop a wide range of transferable skills, including the assimilation, analysis, organisation and synthesis of information and its effective communication in speech and writing, through the study of complex material, which can be applied in a variety of educational and professional contexts, thereby meeting a national and international need for competence in modern foreign languages.

one language to 120 credits (Advanced French, Advanced German, Advanced Italian, Advanced Spanish only) to include departmental optional modules; two languages or one language plus Translation Studies (some languages only allow 40 credits per year, others permit up to 80 credits); three languages or two languages plus Translation Studies
A compulsory period of residence abroad.

Where students taking three languages are exempted from the Year Abroad, the normal expectation would be that the student would only continue with two languages into final year.
Students studying English as a Modern Foreign Language can study:
three languages equally weighted (40/40/40);
two languages equally weighted (60/60);
two languages with one weighted more heavily than the other (80/40).
English can only be combined with Beginners or Advanced French, Beginners or Advanced German, Beginners or Advanced Spanish or Beginners Chinese.

aims: The MSc Global Health System Leadership is aimed at medical and healthcare professionals and policy makers from a variety of non/clinical backgrounds. It is open to all from across the globe but will have a particular focus on those working in the Emirates and neighbouring region. The Eastern Mediterranean Region constitutes 22 countries with diverse situations, many facing conflict and instability and double burden of disease. Additional challenges include climate change, global health security and limitations on public health capacity, which has been magnified during the COVID 19 pandemic. Building a resilient health workforce and systems to advance universal health coverage (UHC) and ensure health security in the Eastern Mediterranean region (EMR) is a top priority.

The MSc Global Health System Leadership works to support health policy development, deliver excellent teaching and put policy into practice by expanding and transforming the health and social care organisation and health workforce within the EMR. Acquiring the knowledge, skills and competencies that speak to the identified nine regional essential public health functions needed to achieve universal health coverage through building resilient health systems and workforce and focusses on extending capabilities in the six global core competencies for UHC. This programme would facilitate the development of knowledge, skills and professional behaviours across these domains through coherent study at Masters Level.

The programme will be attractive to international applicants as there are few opportunities in the Middle East to undertake programmes designed to foster the development of health system and policy experts that are fit-for-purpose and fit-for-practice practitioners to become team leaders, managers, researchers and/or experts. Increasingly there is an expectation from employers that those in middle and senior positions have acquired the attributes inherent in postgraduate study and can demonstrate this through problem solving, supporting, and facilitating other members of the multidisciplinary team and through their leadership in work environments. The modules embedded in the programme structure focus on Global Health Leadership and Management; Global Health Systems and Policy; Strategic Planning; Global Health Economics; Emergency Preparedness Response and Resilience; and Implementation Science.

outcome: Critically analyse and evaluate health systems and policies using theoretical and comparative approaches across different complex, stable and fragile conflict-affected vulnerable settings (FCV), cultures and countries.

Theories, foundational concepts, and context in leadership and management of self, teams, and the organization including concepts of role, power, authority, change and resilience of leaders and managers to develop the knowledge and understanding needed to appraise and evaluate approaches within health systems, complex adaptive systems, and values-based leadership.

Systematic approach to the study of theory and practice of implementation science to recognise, understand and address health system and implementation bottlenecks, identifying, planning, managing and evaluating optimal implementation options for a given setting to improve health system.
