aims: The aim of this programme is to produce Chemical and Formulation Engineers who are equipped to play leading roles in a professional capacity in both industry and academia, and who have developed the technical, intellectual and transferable skills needed to underpin their education and continuing professional development.

MEng graduates will have a systematic knowledge and understanding of Chemical and Formulation Engineering, including developments and problems at the forefront of the discipline.  They will be able to evaluate current research critically, and be original in the application of their knowledge, proposing new hypotheses as appropriate.

Typical MEng graduates will be able to deal with complex issues, making sound judgements in the absence of complete information, and will be able to communicate their conclusions clearly to specialist and non-specialist audiences.  They will be self-motivating and able to act autonomously, and will have the qualities and transferable skills necessary to exercise initiative and personal responsibility, to make decisions in complex and unpredictable situations, and to have the independent learning ability required for continuing professional development.

The high level of numeracy of MEng graduates, and their skills in problem solving, team working, and communication and information technology, equip them for successful careers outside as well as within the process and allied industries.

The honours degree is considerably enhanced when the student is able to augment academic study period through working in an industrial environment, therefore the integration of an industrial placement of one year's duration in the programme aims at the provision of opportunities to see how theoretical and academic work completed within the university environment relates to the practical application in the workplace; enabling students to develop confidence over a significant period of work in skills of organisation, time management and record keeping; and, permitting students to take on gradually more responsibility for the work that they do, so that by the end of the year's placement they are capable to complete a simple element of work from beginning to end with minimal supervision.

2. acquire a comprehensive understanding of techniques applicable to their own research and advanced scholarship.

aims: Theology and religion is a subject area which employs a wide variety of methodological approaches in its discourse. In addition, as well as being an academic subject in its own right, it also has a significance and applicability within communities of faith and other non-academic contexts. The core educational purpose of this programme is to train, equip and inform students concerning this methodological diversity and variety of concerns to prepare graduates for professions which depend upon an advanced awareness of issues of theology and religion or for research in the discipline, and to allow them to better appreciate the significance of issues around theology and religion in contemporary society.

In terms of equipping and informing, students will become critically acquainted with the `sources? of theology: e.g. scriptural writings, historical traditions, doctrinal issues, the importance of the sociological and cultural background (for example, in terms of new `readings? of theology that have emerged out of post-colonial contexts and new insights into biblical scholarship which have arisen from contemporary culture).

In terms of training, students will be encouraged to interrogate and critically analyse their own, and others?, presuppositions and approach their studies in ways that show sensitivity to the multi-disciplinary nature of issues under discussion.

data.shortTitle: LLB Law w Bus St w Yr Abr FT
data.longTitle: Law with Business with Year Abroad
aims: The LLB Law with Business Studies programme provides a broad education in law and in business and opens up career opportunities in many areas. In both the Law and Business parts of the programme, students are encouraged to think for themselves and to adopt a critical and questioning approach.

Lawyers acting for commercial clients can benefit from an understanding of organisations, their management and the way they structure their activities. Men and women in business can benefit from a sound knowledge of the law, particularly of those branches that affect industry and commerce.

Graduates of this degree programme who take up positions as lawyers in company legal departments will have a greater appreciation of their company's overall operations, and of the work done by their colleagues in other departments and divisions, than other law graduates. This will make for better communication and co-operation between their department and other departments in the organisation. Graduates who join solicitors' practices and deal with business clients will have an understanding of the environment in which their clients operate and of the nature of their circumstances and difficulties. Nowadays the organisation and management problems involved in running large law practices are becoming increasingly apparent and occupy a considerable amount of practitioners' time. Law with Business Studies graduates going into private practice will be well equipped to deal with these problems.
For students seeking to become practising lawyers in England & Wales and Northern Ireland, the LLB Law with Business Studies degree gives exemption from the first stage of professional examinations.

Students are exposed to a wide range of approaches to the academic study of law - including the analysis of the creation and application of legal rules, the impact of law on individuals, organisations and society, and the moral and political values expressed in law and legal processes.

The LLB Law with Business Studies programme provides a supportive environment in which students take responsibility for their own learning and aim to become effective life-long learners, with opportunities to review and reflect upon their academic and personal achievements through personal development planning.

Regulation is increasingly transnational and the provision of legal services is increasingly international.  The Year Abroad Option gives students an opportunity to develop a truly globalised outlook by experiencing another academic and legal culture.  The year abroad will also enable students to study a greater range of substantive legal subjects, developed in line with the specific and unique expertise of colleagues at other institutions.

outcome: The legal rules, principles and concepts of the "core" branches of law: Public Law (including constitutional law, administrative law and human rights); Law of the European Union; Criminal Law; Civil Rights and Obligations (including Contract, Tort and Restitution); Property Law.

aims: The programme is managed by the EPSRC funded Centre for Doctoral Training in Formulation Engineering.  The Centre integrates the interdisciplinary expertise of the component schools (Engineering (Chemical Engineering and Materials Science), Physics and Chemistry) aimed at formulation of multiphase structured products in a wide variety of forms.

The programme focuses on research into the physical, chemical and biological processes that create product structure, and the maintenance or breakdown of that structure in use. An important feature of the approach is that it is focused on achieving the desired performance of the product and the means to achieve this, rather than on characterisation of existing processes. This is a different approach from the traditional one in chemical engineering, and places new demands on interdisciplinarity and innovation.

Students will take an inherently multidisciplinary approach, involving the component disciplines of Chemical Engineering, Materials Science, Chemistry, Physics and Biosciences, to a largely undeveloped area. The intention is to develop a framework of understanding for the design, manufacture and performance assessment of formulated products.

Students will develop personal, scientific and business skills to enable them to carry out the joint industry-academia research programme. The programme aims to produce graduates able to take charge of development teams in the most competitive markets.
Previous graduates have progressed to work within the formulation engineering sector, with many continuing employment at their sponsor companies.

data.shortTitle: MA Military History DL
aims: This programme offers an opportunity to study military history at MA level via web-based distance learning. This MA is designed to offer students a rounded and distinctive course, drawing particularly on three of the particular research-led strengths of the University of Birmingham: First World War Studies, Second World War Studies and Air Power Studies. Students will be able to enjoy a unique and multi-faceted learning experience without ever having to leave home.
Specifically, the programme aims;

(1) to provide an advanced understanding of military history for students keen to develop their knowledge and skills in this field, through an attractive series of advanced modules addressing important themes in the discipline.
(2) to enable students to gain and develop both generic and discipline-specific skills, providing a solid base either for further study, or for development of other career opportunities.
(3) to equip students to undertake independent research under supervision, and to write up and present their work to a professional standard.

No other university of comparable standard offers anything quite like this, either in the UK or internationally. The King's College London DL programmes focus almost exclusively on post-1945 and are less historically rigorous than ours will be. Salford has a DL MA with an excellent reputation in Intelligence Studies, but this is more narrowly focussed and the intake is restricted to professionals working in that area. Our closest competitor in every sense looks likely to be Wolverhampton, but the shape of their programme is not yet clear. The sooner we can begin accepting applications for our MA, the less of a threat Wolverhampton will be to our plans.

We have had over 40 direct expressions of interest in such a programme over the course of this year. While not all of those will convert into accepted students, this seems sufficient to assure us that a viable market exists. The fact that our MA will be less expensive than any of our UK competitors should also offer us comfort.

aims: The Educational Aims of the Programme are to:

a) Provide a course designed to meet professionally accredited requirements of study that is of comparable standard to those offered by other leading European universities, that will attract high quality students, irrespective of race, background, gender or physical disability both from within the UK and from overseas;

b) Educate students to MEng (Hons) level, accredited as meeting in full the educational/knowledge and understanding requirement for CEng registration as detailed in the Accreditation of Higher Education Programmes (Fourth edition) (AHEP4);
c) Provide students with a thorough knowledge of engineering principles, concepts and mathematics and with practice at using their understanding to solve complex problems in mechanical engineering;
d) Provide students with a depth of specialised knowledge within a research environment and develop their critical analysis and thinking skills;

e) Enable students to develop the skills necessary to engage in, plan and successfully complete individual and team design projects, and appreciate the economic, social, environmental, ethical and commercial context of their decisions;

f) Produce engineering graduates equipped to play leading roles in industry, the professions and public service, and with the intellectual abilities and transferable skills necessary to further their professional development by personal research or study in preparation for a future career as a registered professional engineer.
Additional aim for students on the 'with Year in Computer Science' programme:

Computer Science is both an academic discipline in its own right and an enabling technology for other disciplines: Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences as well as Science and Engineering. The focus here is firmly on Computer Science as an enabling technology. The programme aims to provide a solid, self-contained and coherent core of computer science suitable for combination with a variety of other academic disciplines. It aims to provide:
1) A grounding in the theory underpinning modern developments in computer science.
2) An introduction to practical software design and implementation.
3) A range of options in computer science to cater for a variety of interests and backgrounds.

outcome: By the end of the programme students will have knowledge and understanding in the specific areas of learning of - Science and Mathematics, Engineering Analysis, Design and Innovation, The Engineer and Society, and Engineering Practice as required by AHEP 4th Edition (Learning outcomes M1-M18). They will specifically have knowledge and understanding of;

1. Mathematics, statistics, natural science and engineering principles for the solution of complex problems in the field of Mechanical Engineering. Much of the knowledge will be at the forefront of the particular subject of study and informed by a critical awareness of new developments and the wider context of engineering. [related to M1]
2. How to formulate and analyse complex problems in Mechanical Engineering to reach substantiated conclusions, and understanding of the limitations of the techniques employed. [related to M2]

data.shortTitle: BA Theology and Religion FT
aims: The programme aims:

To provide students with a framework to think critically about theology and religion via a combination of core and optional modules. No prior knowledge of Theology is required for admission to the programme. Stage I is therefore designed to offer students a broad foundation for the academic study of Theology, and of religion more generally. At Stage II and III the programme seeks to provide a flexible framework by offering a range of diverse options whereby students can develop their own interests, whether this be, for example, in religion and popular culture, issues of race, gender and sexuality in religious and theological perspective, scriptural languages and study of sacred texts, further Sikh, Jewish, or Islamic studies, philosophical and modern theology, or interfaith studies. A central element of Stage III is the requirement that students engage in an extended piece of individual research in a particular area of Theology and Religion (the dissertation).

To enable students to deepen their critical understanding of both classical and contemporary expressions of Christianity and Islamic, Jewish, Hindu and Sikh identity, with a focus on lived experience and the encounter between different faiths. Some modules focus on religious experience and identity in the UK and continental Europe. Others feature a global dimension.

To provide opportunities to develop relevant research skills for a range of theological and study of religion disciplines, to debate philosophical issues and explore some of the ways in which religious themes, ideas, symbols, practices and organisations can be understood in the context of contemporary religious and secular cultures.
To provide students with opportunities to engage with the latest thinking in the subject by drawing upon the range of internationally recognized research undertaken within the department.

To provide students with a range of methodological tools that will equip them for the study of the many different facets of theology and religion. Such tools may include skills of translation and exegesis, the ability to apply sociological, anthropological and archaeological methods of enquiry, analytical skills in reading a range of cultural 'texts' whether these be monuments, films, web presentations etc., critical skills in reading and writing history, skills in identifying issues of race, class, gender and sexuality within religious discourse, and so forth.

To promote effective communication in both oral and written form by developing students? teamwork, presentational, IT, research and analytical skills (particularly in relating theoretical models to practical examples).

aims: This programme will equip university graduates with the knowledge and skills they require to work in the finance sector in Dubai and globally and address their limited knowledge of accounting, economics or finance. The programme gives students a comprehensive and critical knowledge of corporate finance.  It also teaches them how to interpret and analyse financial statements, how to value securities and businesses as well as how to apply a wide range of financial modelling techniques.  This range of knowledge and skills is in high demand in banks, insurance companies, stock broking firms and other industries within the finance sector.  The skills are also in high demand in the treasury departments of many local and multinational companies, government departments and other organisations.  The overall aim of the programme is to produce responsible financial management graduates who will be able to contribute to these organisations in Dubai, the Middle East and globally and craft a career in the sector. Moreover, the programme examines ethics, governance and regulation, as well as the ethics and principles of reporting measures, both internally and externally.  Key accounting regulations which impact on treasury operations are also considered.

The programme is innovative and contemporary, covering topics on financial technology, data analytics and Environmental, Social and Governance financing.  The contemporaneousness of the programme is key in ensuring that its graduates are ready to work in the finance sector globally.

data.shortTitle: MSc AI and Government PT (Dub)
aims: The MSc in AI and Government provides a unique interdisciplinary learning experience at the intersection of technology and public policy. This innovative programme equips students with technical competencies in artificial intelligence alongside contextual understanding of the complexities of government.

Through rigorous training in machine learning, algorithms, programming, statistics, and governance, students gain hard skills to lead development of impactful AI systems. However, the public sector context poses distinct challenges compared to commercial settings. Modules delivered by experts in political science and public administration build awareness of additional considerations around privacy, accountability, stakeholder dynamics, and the political and contested nature of working in the public sector that shape responsible AI adoption and deployment.

The modules introduce the transformative potential alongside heightened risks of these rapidly advancing technologies in the policy sphere. Hands-on projects facilitate learning to address real-world implementation barriers - from procurement to change management - to successfully and ethically embed AI within public organisations. This experiential approach prepares students to drive strategic adoption in complex government environments.

With its blend of technical depth and public sector insight, the programme develops highly skilled professionals ready to pioneer the ethical and effective integration of AI capabilities to enhance governance, deliver public value, and further the public interest. Graduates will lead the responsible transformation of policymaking, service delivery, and regulation in the 21st century.

The key differentiators of the programme are the interdisciplinary nature integrating technical and social science learning, tailored experiential projects applying AI to real public sector contexts, and focus on practical implementation challenges unique to embedding such technologies in government. The key value propositions centre around gaining interdisciplinary expertise tailored to public sector applications, hands-on experiential learning and connections, specialised skills to lead impactful and responsible AI adoption in government and joining a cutting-edge research community focused on the intersection of AI, governance, and policy.

aims: Programme Aims

The aim of the MSc Financial Economics programme is to provide students with thorough training in the core skills and techniques, both theoretical and empirical, needed to understand and analyse the wide range of issues arising across the realm of financial markets and institutions. It also seeks to equip graduates with the quantitative and theoretical tools needed for a successful career in finance as an economist.

As the programme provides specialised instruction in financial economics, it is aimed at students who had previous training in economics and/or finance at the undergraduate level with strong training and foundation in quantitative/empirical methods. Applicants in Economics, a related discipline, or a discipline with a strong quantitative element are encouraged, but they must show strong attainment in quantitative modules at undergraduate level.

The MSc Financial Economics programme will provide the School and University with an opportunity to develop graduates for specialist financial economics career roles in the private sector, and global financial institutions.  In particular, the programme will position its graduates to be compelling candidates to employers in investment and commercial banks, financial asset management companies, financial technology firms, consulting firms, and policy-oriented organizations. Issues relating to financial ethics and sustainability will also be examined on the MSc programme in line with Birmingham Business School’s responsible business ethos.
USP(s) and why students would come to UoB
By enrolling on this programme, students will benefit from:

Being taught by several prominent academics with expertise in various areas of financial economics. Students will gain critical awareness and understanding of the theoretical foundations of financial economics more generally, as well the economics of financial markets and financial institutions in particular.

Being trained in advanced quantitative methods and analytical skills. Students will receive comprehensive training in advanced techniques in dealing with a wide range of issues in the empirical analysis of financial markets and institutions.
Graduate skills and employability
(including areas for future work)
Students on this MSc programme will develop a range of relevant graduate skills, including for example:
development of
expertise in economics, econometrics and/or financial data analysis; strong quantitative skills and experience; evidence of applied financial knowledge and understanding for the workplace.
In terms of wider employability and areas for future work, international career opportunities include a combination of specialist finance career roles, including for example:
financial economist; financial risk analyst; financial market and treasury analyst; financial/ investment analyst; capital market analyst.
Students may also wish to take up further study after completing their Masters programme, e.g. MPhil/PhD.

aims: The Birmingham Award with Distinction / The Birmingham Dubai Award with Distinction is a co-curricular programme that students undertake alongside their degree to develop, recognise, and articulate the attributes that they have developed at Birmingham, in preparation for the graduate recruitment and development processes.

The programme offers a flexible approach to skill development through the formal recognition of both on-and off campus extra-curricular activities, including those from all Colleges, Professional Services, and the Guild of Students.

This provision includes quality-assured structured teaching sessions that allow a learner to explore and develop a deeper understanding of a skill area through classroom-based teaching sessions, and digital education materials, co-created with employer partners.

Each activity recognised by The Birmingham Award will be required to identify the responsibilities of the role/activity and identify between one and four of the institutional Graduate Attributes that a student can develop as a result of engaging. A student will be required to participate in four activities, and for each activity, will need to identify an achievement or career progression goal from engagement, to be eligible to complete the award.

All students are required to complete a compulsory educational programme and associated summative assessments designed to prepare a learner for the graduate recruitment and development process. Each student receives personalised feedback on their assessment to ensure the transformative approach to the curriculum.

aims: This unique programme aims to support students to:
gain knowledge and competency in the theory and practice of systems thinking
develop as a system thinking practitioner, capable of exercising effective systems leadership.

The inclusion of systems leadership alongside more formal systems thinking practitioner capacities and skills is unique to this programme.  Combining knowledge and skills with leadership development is at the core of the Birmingham Leadership Institute's (BLI) strategy. The learning outcomes enable practitioners to apply systems thinking tools and techniques in a sophisticated way by utilising adaptive leadership capacities ensuring wider stakeholder engagement and more effective systems diagnosis, design and interventions. Systems thinking, leadership and development are integrated throughout all the modules.

Theories of human sense making and perception including attention, bias and emotions, their relevance to systems thinking and leadership practice.

In rapidly evolving global contexts, intercultural communication provides an essential set of competences that enable successful communication in the diverse workplaces that global companies are familiar with and the diverse environments in which we live. The programme aims to develop your understanding of the challenges of achieving effective communication in international professional and interpersonal settings. data.shortTitle: BA History wih Soc Anth FT
aims: This programme combines the study of social anthropology and history.

The social anthropology side of the programme provides students with a comprehensive overview of the discipline of social anthropology, incorporating theoretical and methodological training, and covering a range of topics and sub-fields. Students will gain an understanding of the historical development of the discipline through a syllabus that brings together widely acknowledged anthropological thinkers and schools of thought with critical voices and perspectives. The programme aims to develop an innovative range of transferable skills in research, analysis and presentation, alongside an appreciation of the diversity of contemporary human cultures and societies.

The history side of the programme provides students the opportunity to acquire an understanding of historical events and processes - and of the enduring legacies of the past ? across a range of topics that span diverse chronologies (from the Bronze Age to the present day). geographies and scales (from the West Midlands to Africa, Asia, and the Americas). In so doing, the programme develops a range of analytical and organisational skills, independent and critical thinking, and the ability to synthesise and communicate information and ideas. These attributes will be developed through three interlocked strands of the curriculum:

? Studying History through which students will develop a specialist knowledge of particular historical topics that span a range of periods (from the ancient world to the present day), of geographies (from the local to the global), and themes;
? Understanding History through which students will develop an understanding of the theoretical and methodological development of the discipline and its place in contemporary culture and society;
? and Doing History through which students will undertake original historical research both as an individual and as part of a team.

The programme also attunes students to contemporary challenges within and beyond the discipline - globalisation; sustainability; inequalities ? and to the importance of thinking critically about heritage, conservation, and the place of the past in public life. As such, diversity is the heart of the curriculum. The programme recovers and reintegrates the voices of those previously marginalised by virtue of race, gender, sexuality, (dis)ability, or excluded by virtue of dominant narratives of the past and enables and encourages students to explore the histories and cultures of different peoples, societies, and cultures from around the world. The programme challenges students to engage with communities in the city, the region, and beyond.

Graduates will display a broad knowledge of social anthropology and history and be able to demonstrate intellectual versatility and organisational flexibility. The programme will encourage independent and critical thinking, culminating in a dissertation based on supervised independent research in the final year of study in either social anthropology or history.

The programme will prepare students for a wide range of careers and will provide a sound base for further study in social anthropology, history or related disciplines. Students will develop the transferable skills that are associated with all arts, humanities and social science degree programmes, including: identification of areas of enquiry and relevant sources of information; referencing, evaluation, synthesis and analysis of information in the light of relevant methodological and theoretical frameworks; clear and coherent communication in person and on paper.
(See 'Other Information' for details relating to the Year Abroad)

outcome: A body of historical information characterised by geographical range, thematic breadth and chronological depth
A range of sources available to historians? including, but not limited to, textual primary evidence ? and an awareness of both their value and their limitations.
The historiographical development of core debates in history, and an appreciation of the reasons for continued controversies;
The conceptual, theoretical, and ideological influences on historical events and processes, and on their interpretation.
The enduring legacies of the past and the relevance of historical knowledge and understanding to the interpretation of contemporary events.
The scope, range and history of social anthropology

aims: To enable students to achieve the appropriate level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (specified by language under Learning Outcomes) through the systematic integration of language and content teaching.
To enable students to explain and assess critically the multi-disciplinary features and significance of the culture, history and society of their chosen language communities.

To enable students to be digitally literate. Students will be able to use appropriate, up-to-date technology in the effective learning of languages and to understand works of culture (understood in the broadest sense, to include history, society, politics, and other material covered in modules aligned with the Birmingham Languages Graduate).
To enable students to handle and analyse material relating to research projects based in the Department of Modern Languages.
*To enable students to engage with appropriately adapted questions derived from research projects based in the Department of Modern Languages.
To enable students to become effective independent learners, with regular opportunities to develop skills in research, academic writing, and reflective learning.

To enable students to be competitively employable through the acquisition of direct and transferable skills as well as through: 1) appropriate integration of Modern Languages careers topics within core modules; 2) optional placement opportunities relating to Modern Languages (credit-bearing and non-credit-bearing); 3) non-credit bearing Modern Languages careers events.
*To enable students to give a persuasive account of their degree and of why they have assembled their degree in a particular way.

To provide students with language and language-related transferable skills useful in a range of contexts, both educational and professional; and to respond to national and international needs for advanced strategic competence in a variety of world languages.
To enable students to acquire first-hand experience of living and studying and/ or working abroad.

To enable students to develop a wide range of transferable skills, including the assimilation, analysis, organisation and synthesis of information and its effective communication in speech and writing, through the study of complex material, which can be applied in a variety of educational and professional contexts, thereby meeting a national and international need for competence in modern foreign languages.
Students  can study:

one language to 120 credits (Advanced French, Advanced German, Advanced Italian, Advanced Spanish only) to include departmental optional modules; two languages or one language plus Translation Studies (some languages only allow 40 credits per year, others permit up to 80 credits); three languages or two languages plus Translation Studies
A compulsory period of residence abroad.

Exemption from the year abroad: In exceptional circumstances, students may be granted an exemption from the compulsory year abroad. Where students taking three languages are exempted from the Year Abroad, the normal expectation would be that the student would only continue with two languages into final year.
Students studying English as a Modern Foreign Language can study:
three languages equally weighted (40/40/40);
two languages equally weighted (60/60);
two languages with one weighted more heavily than the other (80/40).
English can only be combined with Beginners or Advanced French, Beginners or Advanced German, Beginners or Advanced Spanish or Beginners Chinese.
The following languages cannot be taken together for timetabling reasons:
Pillar 1: English as a Modern Foreign Language (EMFL), Italian, Japanese and Russian
Pillar 2: Chinese Mandarin, German and Portuguese
Pillar 4: French and Catalan Minor
Translation Studies with Advanced Russian as your only Advanced language. Languages in the same pillar cannot be taken together.

aims: This programme provides a comprehensive overview of the discipline of Social Anthropology, incorporating theoretical and methodological training, and covering a wide range of topics and sub-fields. Students will gain an appreciation of the historical development of the discipline, with a view to incorporating lesser-known voices and perspectives alongside widely acknowledged anthropological thinkers and schools of thought. The programme aims to develop an innovative range of transferable skills in research, analysis and presentation through the study and understanding of human cultures and societies from around the world. The programme will facilitate intellectual development by encouraging independent and critical thinking, culminating in an independent research dissertation in the final year of study. The programme will prepare students for a wide range of careers and will provide a sound base for further study in Social Anthropology. Students will develop the transferable skills that are associated with all arts, humanities and social science degree programmes, including: identification of areas of enquiry and relevant sources of information; referencing, evaluation, synthesis and analysis of information in the light of relevant methodological and theoretical frameworks; clear and coherent communication in person and on paper.
For semester/year abroad only:

Study abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. The year abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.

outcome: 1. The scope, range and history of social anthropology

3. The multifaceted nature of social anthropology and its complex relationships to other disciplines

5. The importance of empirical fieldwork as the primary method of gathering data and as a basis for the generation of anthropological theory and the comparative study of human societies
6. The nature and extent of human diversity and commonality, and different explanations that have been offered for this diversity.
7. The ethical issues entailed in the study of social worlds and the representation of others, and the potential applications and misapplications of Anthropology.
8. Demonstrate the ability to study relevant topics at an international institution and appreciate the difference between study in the UK and overseas. (Only applicable to students studying abroad)

aims: This programme provides students with an understanding of economic concepts, principles and tools, with a particular focus on mathematical and statistical methods. The programme aims to stimulate students intellectually through the study of economics and to lead them to appreciate its application to a range of problems and its relevance in a variety of contexts. Students should receive a firm foundation of knowledge about the workings of economic systems and develop the relevant skills for the constructive use of that knowledge in a range of settings.

The first year of the programme provides a foundation in economics and a rigorous grounding in mathematics and statistics. The second year develops a core of Microeconomics, Macroeconomics and Econometrics, alongside more specialised policy-based and theoretical modules. The third year is spent studying in a country where classes are conducted in English. Students gain an improved understanding of the cultural context of economics in another country. If they wish they can study modules in Economics taught in the language of the country, if available at the institution. In the final year of the programme, there is more advanced coverage of econometrics and mathematical economics together with increased flexibility to specialise in a number of theoretical and policy-oriented fields.

The programme provides students with advanced mathematical and technical skills that are applicable to the study of Economics and transferable to other areas, including analytical skills and an ability to develop simplifying frameworks for studying the real world. On graduating, students will be well prepared to work in a range of graduate careers, for example in banking, finance or general management careers, or to progress to Masters-level study in Economics.

outcome: 1. Economic concepts and principles addressing microeconomic issues, such as consumption, production, markets and market failure, economic welfare, and macroeconomic issues, such as employment, national income, the balance of payments, economic growth, business cycles, and the role of the financial system in the economy.

2. Relevant advanced quantitative methods and tools for data analysis including appropriate mathematical and statistical methods, computational techniques and econometrics, taking into account compliance with data usage regulations.

3. Relevant theoretical, model-based and empirical analytical tools, and different methodological approaches to the analysis of economic policy and applications of relevant economic principles and reasoning.
4. Application of economic principles, their mathematical formulation, and the statistical means by which theories and propositions can be evaluated to a variety of topics.
5. Relevant verbal, graphical, mathematical and econometric representations and communication of economic ideas and analysis, in various relevant media.

aims: Students will gain knowledge of a range of fundamental and modern statistical principles and techniques along with data analysis skills. This will enable students to develop and apply various statistical models including by using computational techniques using statistical software. These statistical problem-solving skills will be applicable to various current problems giving insights at the forefront of the field. Presentation skills both in written and verbal form will be developed alongside an ability to work professionally and independently.

There is a national shortage of personnel who are highly qualified in statistics.  This shortage is set to grow in the future. Such personnel are vital to many sectors, for example economics, medicine, finance, insurance and industrial management. This programme aims to address this shortage by producing highly qualified students who will have the ability to integrate the knowledge of statistics to address, analyse and provide a rational appraisal of a problem.  In particular, the aims of the proposed programme are to provide high quality personnel having the skills:
a) to be able to understand statistical theory and carry out critical analysis of a problem based on the fundamental principles of statistics,
b) to be able to use statistical software packages to carry out statistical analysis,
c) and to be able to apply a range of statistical techniques in broader and unfamiliar environments.

outcome: Fundamental principles of statistical concepts and theory.

aims: The MSc in Urban Analytics for Planners is designed to equip students with advanced skills in data analysis and modelling, with a specific focus on their application to urban planning and transport systems. This programme emphasises the integration of quantitative methods with urban theory and practice, preparing students to address the complex challenges that cities face in an increasingly data-driven world. At the core of the programme is a focus on using data analytics to inform smart urban planning decisions that enhance sustainability, mobility, and the overall quality of urban life.

Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of the role of data in shaping urban environments, from the collection and analysis of large datasets to the application of spatial models and visualization techniques. This programme will attract individuals from diverse backgrounds, including planners, engineers, and data scientists, who are eager to leverage their technical expertise to address pressing urban issues. Through a combination of theoretical study and practical application, students will be prepared to lead in the development of data-driven solutions for cities, ensuring that their designs are not only functional but also sustainable and resilient.

Throughout the programme, students will first build a solid foundation in urban planning before progressing to specialised tools and practical skills in urban analytics. In the second semester, students will collaborate with peers from related disciplines in an integrated Urban Lab, working on real-world urban projects. This hands-on experience, supervised by industry professionals, will equip students with the practical skills and professional insight necessary to excel in the growing field of urban analytics.

Graduates of the MSc Data Analytics for Urban Planners programme will be uniquely positioned for careers at the intersection of data science, transport planning, and urban planning and development. As cities increasingly rely on data-driven solutions to address mobility, sustainability, and growth challenges, graduates will be highly sought after for roles in government agencies, consultancy firms, urban analytics companies, and transport planning organisations. Their ability to apply advanced data analytics to complex urban systems will make them key contributors to the future of urban planning and design. To achieve this, all modules will take an interdisciplinary approach, ensuring that graduates can articulate the science behind critical urban issues, and confidently offer solutions. As a result, graduates of this programme will be highly sought after, not only in traditional planning roles within consultancies and government agencies but also in NGOs, international organizations (e.g., World Bank, UN), and emerging sustainability sectors within large corporations.

aims: The PGDip aims to introduce students to classical and advanced management concepts through a combination of core foundation subjects, and also a number of elective choices.

The PGDip will build on students? managerial experience, enabling them to develop the breadth of knowledge, understanding and skills required to deal with the complexities of management and leadership in an international context. The MBA will prepare students for a senior leadership role in managing change in organisations.
The specific objectives of the programme are to develop:
1. An understanding of leadership and the development of leadership practice
2. An understanding of and ability to develop and implement strategy
3. An understanding of the factors involved in international business
4. An understanding of how to undertake corporate internationalisation
5. A foundation of business knowledge through an integrated appreciation of Marketing, Operations, HRM and Accounting and Finance
6. Student confidence and capability in business leadership through multiple group projects within a range of organisational contexts in the UK and overseas.

outcome: 1) Organisations, the business environment in which they operate and their management. How organisations can respond to and shape the dynamic and changing nature of business. (QAA benchmark ? 3.2)

aims: This Taught LLM programme enables graduate students, both from within the European Union and elsewhere, to develop expertise in a variety of subjects in which the School of Law has significant strengths. This taught LLM programme provides a supportive environment in which students take responsibility for their own learning and aim to become effective life long learners.
The programme aims:

1.  to enable students to acquire a systematic understanding of the subjects they study, and a critical awareness of current problems and/or new insights, much of which is at, or informed by, the forefront of the subjects studied.
2. to enable students to acquire a comprehensive understanding of techniques applicable to their own research and advanced scholarship.

3. to encourage students to demonstrate originality in the application of knowledge, together with a practical understanding of how established techniques of research and enquiry are used to create and interpret knowledge in the discipline.
4. to enable students to acquire a conceptual understanding that allows them to evaluate critically current research and advanced scholarship in the discipline.
5 to enable students to develop their skills in research and writing through preparing assessed work and a substantial dissertation written under the supervision of a specialist in the subject.

outcome: 1. A cross-cutting range of fields of law from a list of all modules offered on all LLM programmes and which can cover all or parts of: criminal law and criminal justice, public law, regulation and governance, international and comparative law, commercial law, economic and trade law, environmental and energy law, human rights law, European law, healthcare law and socio-legal studies. (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
2. The significance of social, political, economic or commercial contexts in which legal rules and principles operate; (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
3. Comparisons to be drawn between areas of the Law being studied and the Law as it has developed in other jurisdictions where appropriate; (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)

4. The role and importance of persuasive analysis to law and the range of theories that can be applied to offer evidenced conclusions, addressing complex actual or hypothetical problems; and (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
5. Proposals to reform the areas of Law being studied. (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
learning: Seminars, lectures and individual assistance with written work
assessment: For all qualifications: Assessed essays; and/or written examinations and/ or presentations; and, for those completing LLM qualification, a dissertation.

outcome: 1. To carry out practical legal research using information technology and paper-based sources (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
2. To bring together relevant material from primary and secondary sources (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)

3. To produce academic writing to a high standard of scholarship, including writing effectively in the English language and presenting information and ideas in a manner that meets relevant academic conventions (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)

4. To apply legal and related knowledge systematically to complex problems by constructing arguments, recognising potential alternative conclusions and providing supporting reasons (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
5. To communicate effectively, by giving and receiving information and ideas and modifying responses where appropriate (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
6. To think critically and creatively about matters covered in the programme, demonstrating a capacity for independent thinking (LLM, PGDip, PGCert)
learning: Individual research supervision for dissertation on a legal topic; guidance in seminars in relation to assessed essays. Active participation in seminars; self-directed use of communication skills training offered by The University of Birmingham.
assessment: For all qualifications: Assessed essays; and/or written examinations and/ or presentations; and,
for those completing LLM qualification, a dissertation.

aims: Sustainability is increasingly becoming a core aspect of all engineering and physical sciences, and chemistry is essential to help society to achieve a sustainable future.  The aim of this postgraduate programme is to educate students in advanced aspects of sustainable chemistry while also providing them with the skills and knowledge required to develop a career in an increasingly sustainability-focused chemical sector.
In more detail, the programme aims to:
Provide a sound knowledge base in the field of sustainable chemistry, to provide a grounding in the fundamentals of sustainability and to develop wider transferable skills;
Provide a rational, structured and coherent programme of study that is relevant to the needs of employers;
Facilitate the professional development of the student and provide training in appropriate skills (e.g., laboratory skills and chemical safety);
Develop a logical and enquiring attitude, with appropriate critical analysis and scientific discipline to encourage lifelong learning;
Provide experience of originality in the application of knowledge and understanding of how research techniques are used to create and interpret knowledge in sustainable chemistry;
Develop an enthusiasm for sustainable chemistry, and expose students to the frontiers of the discipline;
Generate in students an appreciation of the importance of the application of sustainability principles in industrial, economic, environmental and social contexts;
Provide an enhanced research experience through completion of a research project.

outcome: Life-cycle assessment;

Green chemistry;
Materials for energy storage;

Sustainable polymer chemistry;
Scientific communication skills;
Research methodology.
learning: The acquisition of knowledge is achieved mainly through lectures and directed student-centred learning.
Support of lecture-based learning is provided by workshops.

assessment: Assessment methods as specified in each module guide.  All learning outcomes in a module are assessed, and the mode of assessment specified for each outcome.
In general, modules are assessed by a combination of continuous assessment during the year and written unseen examinations.

outcome: The ability to integrate theoretical concepts and practice;
The ability to synthesise information and data from a variety of sources;
The ability to put forward and test hypotheses;
The ability to apply chemical and sustainability principles to the solution of complex problems;
The ability to analyse, evaluate and interpret the results of controlled experiments;
The ability to demonstrate the skills necessary to plan, conduct and report a substantial research project;
The ability to evaluate critically current research in sustainability and evaluate methodologies.
learning: Intellectual skills are developed through the integration of theoretical material, assignments and project work.  Open-ended project work is designed to allow students to demonstrate achievement of the overall learning outcomes in a synoptic fashion.
assessment: Partly through written unseen examinations, but the main vehicle for assessment of intellectual skills is in the continuous assessment components and the written report associated with the research project.

aims: To train high quality patient-oriented pharmacy graduates who will have an integrated scientific understanding of medicines and clinical knowledge, enabling them to optimise the safe and effective use of medicines at a patient and population level.
To produce confident professionals who have the ability to communicate the results of their clinical and professional decision making to the healthcare team, patients and the public.

To produce graduates and registrants with a commitment to life-long learning and development, innovation in practice and the skills to create, evaluate and implement new evidence and science to work with patients and the public to improve outcomes and enhance their care.

To produce a cohort of pharmacy graduates and registrants who will provide clinical leadership within all branches of the profession of pharmacy and can contribute to patient care upon registration with the ability to assess patients and prescribe independently.
To provide an integrated knowledge base, progressing throughout the modules, allowing students to demonstrate their application of knowledge and appropriate level of mastery of competencies.

aims: Programme Aims:

The BA History and Politics provides students the opportunity to acquire expertise in two cognate disciplines and, moreover, challenges them to think beyond intellectual boundaries and to synthesise information and insights from both sides of their degree.

On the History side of the programme, students develop an understanding of historical events and processes – and of the enduring legacies of the past – across a range of topics that span a diverse range of chronologies (from the Bronze Age to the present day) and geographies and scales (from the West Midlands to Africa, Asia, and the Americas). In so doing, the programme develops a range of analytical and organisational skills, independent and critical thinking, and the ability to synthesise and communication information and ideas. These attributes will be developed through three interlocked strands of the curriculum:
- Studying History

through which students will develop a specialist knowledge of particular historical topics that span a range of periods (from the ancient world to the present day), of geographies (from the local to the global), and themes;
- Understanding History
through which students will develop an understanding of the theoretical and methodological development of the discipline and its place in contemporary culture and society;
- and
Doing History
through which students will undertake original historical research both as an individual and as part of a team.

The History side of the programme also attunes students to contemporary challenges within and beyond the discipline – globalisation; sustainability; inequalities – to the importance of thinking critically about heritage, conservation, and the place of the past in public life. The programme recovers and reintegrates the voices of those previously marginalised by virtue of race, gender, sexuality, (dis)ability, or excluded by virtue of dominant narratives of the past and enables and encourages students to explore the histories and cultures of different peoples, societies, and cultures from around the world and diversity, in the broadest sense of the term, sits at the heart of the curriculum.

On the Politics side of the programme, too, diversity is central to the study of political analysis and of political theory.  While students receive a foundation in three vital elements of the discipline – in the scope and contested nature of political analysis; in political thought and political theory; in the tools of political analysis – these core skills are applied and developed through a wide selection of optional modules that focus on more specialised aspects of politics and political analysis and that, as in History, encompass local, national, international, and global issues.

The programme facilitates the development of a wide and diverse range of transferable skills – in research, in analysis, in evaluation, in organisation, and in communication – and, in particular, the dual nature of the programme enables students to develop specific high-level skills in intellectual synthesis and the ability to think across conventional boundaries. The programme thus prepares students both for further study and for a wide range of careers beyond the academy.
For year abroad programmes only:

The year abroad will provide students with the opportunity to immerse themselves in the society and culture of a foreign country while gaining experience of a different academic environment and way of teaching. The year abroad also provides an opportunity for students to improve their existing language proficiency (where applicable) as well as enhancing their organisation and communication skills and their employability through a proven ability to succeed in a foreign setting.

aims: The Year in Modern Languages will:
Help you become a confident language user, reaching a recognised level of fluency in your chosen language.
Give you the tools to explore and question the culture, history, and society behind the languages you study?and come to your own informed opinions.
Build your awareness of different cultures and perspectives, helping you connect with people and ideas from around the world.
Support you in becoming an independent learner, with strong skills in research, academic writing, and reflecting on your progress.
Prepare you for the world of work by developing practical and transferable skills?and offering career-focused events to help you plan your future.
Offer opportunities (like an optional, short summer study placement abroad) so you can put your language skills into action and experience life in another culture.
Help you confidently explain your degree, your interests, and the choices you?ve made'so you can stand out to employers.
Equip you with language and communication skills you can use in lots of careers, responding to the growing global demand for people who can think and work across languages and cultures.

outcome: The advanced strategic usage of one or two modern languages including the linguistic structures of the languages. By the end of the year students taking `Advanced? modules in French, German, or Spanish should have achieved at least B1 level and normally B2 level within the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. By the end of the year students taking Beginner modules in Catalan, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Mandarin Chinese, Spanish, Portuguese, and Russian should have achieved at least A1 and normally A2. Students should be able to select and use appropriate, up-to-date technology in the effective learning of languages.

The features and significance of the culture, history and society of their chosen language communities. Students should be able to use appropriate, up-to-date technology in such understanding. Dependent on the range of optional modules offered, specialised further topics within Modern Languages such as translation, politics, cinema, history, society or culture.

Knowledge of the society and culture of the countries where the language is spoken.
The significance of language and languages to our connections to other peoples and places around the globe, and in our own lives.  This understanding will (a) span multiple disciplines and (b) extend across times, places, and identities, including with regards to:The historical and contemporary significance of different languages and cultures.Cultural responses to the urgent human.
learning: Modules are taught by specialist staff using various styles and contexts. Beginners have an intensive language course. Support materials are available online and on campus.
Language and content modules are taught weekly, with technology integrated at all levels. Teaching methods include plenaries, seminars, language classes, tutorials and independent reading.
assessment: Assessment methods include coursework, which could take the form of essays, project work, recorded oral presentations, target language projects and portfolios; unseen written exams, oral/aural exams; and tasks under timed conditions.
Associated formative e-tasks and student-led research are also part of the evaluation process.

outcome: Comprehension, analysis, evaluation, distillation and contextualisation of information across a range of subject areas and the application of both generic and subject specific skills.

Ability to summarise, synthesise, analyse and evaluate others? arguments, and to formulate their own logical and structured arguments, normally both orally and in writing, with appropriate supporting evidence, both in English and in the target language(s)

Independent study skills (self-organisation, initiative and self-direction; time management; autonomous research skills; the ability to collect, organise, synthesise and evaluate information; planning, drafting and editing)
Intercultural awareness, understanding and competence and to engage critically with their own and other cultures

Generic, transferable language-learning skills and the ability to use language reference materials such as grammars, standard and specialised dictionaries, and in some cases corpora to refine knowledge and understanding of register, nuances of meaning and language use.
learning: Students attend lectures, engage with online resources, read, and contribute to seminars and tutorials. They complete regular written exercises and use the University Library, IT, and other information sources.

Target language seminars involve extensive reading and practice. Language work and content modules require independent application of techniques taught in classes. Problem-Based Learning, presentations, group projects, and independent learning are integral.
Teaching methods include formative assessments, seminars, tutorials, and group work.
assessment: Coursework: Essays, project work, oral presentations, target language projects, e-assessment portfolios, recorded presentations.

aims: "This programme is for students who have been granted an exemption from the compulsory year abroad on the 4-year 5099 BA Modern Languages programme. Where students taking three languages are exempted from the Year Abroad, the normal expectation would be that the student would only continue with two languages into final year.
Programme aims for students who commenced their studies before 2017/18:

To provide students with language and language-related transferable skills useful in a range of contexts, both educational and professional; and to respond to national and international needs for advanced strategic competence in a variety of world languages.
To enable students to acquire knowledge and understanding of features of the culture, history and society of their chosen language communities.
Programme aims marked with an * apply to new year 1 students entering in 2017/18 onwards

*To enable students to achieve the appropriate level of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (specified by language under Learning Outcomes) through the systematic integration of language and content teaching.
*To enable students to explain and assess critically the multi-disciplinary features and significance of the culture, history and society of their chosen language communities.

*To enable students to be digitally literate. Students will be able to use appropriate, up-to-date technology in the effective learning of languages and to understand works of culture (understood in the broadest sense, to include history, society, politics, and other material covered in modules aligned with the Birmingham Languages Graduate).
*To enable students to handle and analyse material relating to research projects based in the Department of Modern Languages.
*To enable students to engage with appropriately adapted questions derived from research projects based in the Department of Modern Languages.
*To enable students to become effective independent learners, with regular opportunities to develop skills in research, academic writing, and reflective learning.

*To enable students to be competitively employable through the acquisition of direct and transferable skills as well as through: 1) appropriate integration of Modern Languages careers topics within core modules; 2) optional placement opportunities relating to Modern Languages (credit-bearing and non-credit-bearing); 3) non-credit bearing Modern Languages careers events.
*To enable students to give a persuasive account of their degree and of why they have assembled their degree in a particular way.

*To provide students with language and language-related transferable skills useful in a range of contexts, both educational and professional; and to respond to national and international needs for advanced strategic competence in a variety of world languages.
Programme aims for all students:

To enable students to develop a wide range of transferable skills, including the assimilation, analysis, organisation and synthesis of information and its effective communication in speech and writing, through the study of complex material, which can be applied in a variety of educational and professional contexts, thereby meeting a national and international need for competence in modern foreign languages.

Students can study: three languages equally weighted (40/40/40); two languages equally weighted (60/60); two languages with one weighted more heavily than the other (80/40); or a single language to 120 credits where available (Advanced French, Advanced German, Advanced or Beginners Italian, Advanced Spanish)to include departmental optional modules.

year1.yearText: Students can study:Route 1: A Major in RussianStudents study Russian alongside one modern foreign language. In all years of study, they must take a minimum of 80 credits in Russian and 40 credits in the modern foreign language. NB Catalan and Mandarin Chinese can only be studied on Route 1 (Major in Russian).Students take all compulsory core language modules in their relevant languages as described below, plus further credits appropriate to their level (beginners or advanced). Route 2: A Joint Honours in Russian Students study Russian alongside one modern foreign language. Students must take a minimum of 60 credits in Russian and 60 credits in one modern foreign language in Year 1. In Year 2 and Final Year, students can vary their credit weighting.Students take all compulsory core language modules in their relevant languages as described below, plus further credits appropriate to their level (beginners or advanced).With the approval of relevant staff (normally the Director of Undergraduate Studies and/ or Admissions Tutor, in consultation with teaching colleagues, according to module availability) students may seek to change the number and weighting of their languages at appropriate points in the degree (e.g. once end-of-stage results are confirmed). NB students may not normally pick up a supplementary language after the standard course change period at the start of Stage I, even if they have A Levels or equivalent in all relevant languages.The University Regulations state that the minimum requirement for a named specialist minor (Route 1) is 100 credits. In order to reach 100 credits in a language (French, German, Italian, Portuguese and Spanish) you must undertake all core language modules (which will total 90 credits) and make up the additional credits with the Core V Research Project, the Independent Study Module or optional modules in the relevant languages.

aims: The overall aim of the programme is to enable exploration of the theoretical basis of exercise and sports medicine in general and football in particular, and its application to the development of a physiotherapist's and doctor's clinical reasoning. Using the process of clinical reasoning as its framework, the programme will integrate the key issues central to practice in this specialist area, including: clinical assessment, communication skills, accurate diagnosis, differential diagnosis, diagnostics and prognostics, treatment interventions, management approaches, best evidence, evaluation of outcome, strategies to reduce injury time etc. The programme will facilitate the evaluation of existing evidence through the exploration of the assessment and management of athletes. It will provide students with the opportunity to tailor their learning experience to meet their personal and professional needs, developing their capacity for leadership within an interdisciplinary team providing clinical management in elite sport. The programme will promote enquiry based learning through a range of strategies including case analysis and Problem Based Learning.

aims: This MSc in Urban Planning and Regional Development addresses the complex and evolving challenges of urban development through a multi and inter-disciplinary lens. Drawing on the University of Birmingham's internationally recognised expertise in Urban Design and Planning, Environmental Science, and Critical Urban Studies, the programme equips students with essential knowledge, analytical tools, and practical skills to work across government, the private sector, NGOs, and communities.

Central to the programme is an understanding of planning as a spatial, social, economic, legal, and environmental practice. The curriculum integrates social science as an analytical framework to explore how planning decisions shape communities, economies, and built environments. Key areas of focus include the interplay between land use and transportation, the design and realisation of place, and the legal and institutional frameworks that structure plan-making and development control. Students also gain insight into economic development processes, including infrastructure and real estate dynamics, alongside major environmental challenges such as transitions to post-carbon urban futures.

The programme provides a strong foundation in planning theory and governance, progressing through policy development, spatial strategy, and advanced research methods. Set within the UAE's rapidly urbanising context, shaped by ambitious development agendas and global aspirations for sustainable and smart cities, the curriculum offers an applied and internationally relevant learning experience. It addresses pressing urban planning and design challenges such as smart and sustainable placemaking, integrated infrastructure provision, masterplanning, and the design of inclusive public spaces. Place-based thinking underpins all modules, enabling students to develop spatially coherent and socially responsive strategies that inform integrated policy and plan-making.

A distinctive feature of the programme is its practice-based Urban Lab project, where students collaborate across disciplines with peers from the MSc in Sustainable Urban Design and MSc in Urban Analytics and AI for Planners. Working with public and private stakeholders, students co-develop solutions to real-world planning problems. The learning experience is enriched by site visits, fieldwork, practitioner talks, and studio-based design and analysis work.
Core skills and knowledge areas include:
Designing inclusive, healthy, and liveable urban environments
Evaluating infrastructure systems and planning across scales
Understanding global urban trends and emerging technologies
Addressing socio-spatial inequality, migration, and community resilience
Navigating legal and institutional dimensions of planning

Assessments are rooted in real-world case studies and authentic tasks, preparing students for the realities of professional planning. Graduates will emerge as confident practitioners, able to translate evidence into policy, apply design-led thinking, and contribute to sustainable urban development.

The programme prepares students for careers in government, planning consultancies, infrastructure firms, development agencies, and global organisations such as the UN and World Bank, meeting the growing demand for planners who can lead the development of equitable, resilient, and well-governed urban regions.

outcome: 1. The theory and practice of urban and regional planning

4. The opportunities and threats posed to urban areas by globalisation, new technologies and the speed of change.  The impact of urban growth on the natural environment such as atmospheric pollution, water quality etc and the various approaches that are under development to mitigate them. assessment: Essays, presentations, case study reports, urban design plans and the extended research project

aims: Birmingham Business School aims to deliver a learning that is relevant to our executive MBA student's day-to-day work, under the ethos of transforming knowledge from all core business disciplines into practice and new behaviours.
This programme aims to develop responsible, reflective, and resilient business leaders for the promotion of sustainable futures who by the end of the programme will be able to:

1. Integrate and apply critical knowledge and competencies and develop effective governance structures and partnerships to lead, manage and respond to local, regional, and global challenges in a responsible and sustainable way.
2. Demonstrate the skills required for evidence-informed and culturally sensitive and contextual decision making in the changing world of work and business.
3. Continuously broaden their own mindset to sustainably innovate and perform effectively in complex, uncertain and changing business environments.
4. Lead and manage purposefully and inclusively within their organisation and in their interactions with a diverse set of external stakeholders.
5. Demonstrate a creative and entrepreneurial mindset for the development of a sustainable future.
6. Apply relevant knowledge to inspire future organisational strategies.
7. Continuously adapt and develop professionally.

Aiming to deliver an integrative learning experience and the opportunity for our students to focus on their own development in a purposeful way through three elements of learning that makes this programme distinctive.

The first element is the Purposeful Leader module. This module will provide an opportunity for our students to focus on their personal and professional development and to support them with the objectives they have for their career beyond the executive MBA. Students will have the opportunity to reflect on their career ambitions and discuss how those ambitions will inform the choice of final project. In this exercise students will be nurtured to choose a final project which suits their values and career aspirations.

The second distinctive element of learning is the integrative nature of the Global Perspectives on Responsible Business module. This module combines applied learning with values and principles of responsible business and creates and opportunity for a no-boundaries problem assessment and solving approach to develop responsible and sustainable solutions to business issues.

The third distinctive element is the exciting avenues that elective* modules open to our students. As part of the programme students will choose four (4) optional modules from a variety of subjects, types of modules and locations (subject to availability and additional requirements). When choosing electives, students can specialise their degree. The specialisations available are Innovation & Business Transformation, Marketing, and International Business & Strategy.

Through the learning journey we expect that our executive MBA students will develop a range of skills such as analytical skills relevant for business decision making negotiation, communications, leadership, digital skills, interpersonal skills, and stakeholders? management skills.

Finally, aiming to provide our graduates with tangible networking and lifelong learning opportunities, our alumni network will offer opportunities to stay connected with the school and remain at the forefront of business practice and knowledge, for example by being invited to:
join the MBA a regular roundtable discussions and networking opportunities.
join one of the standard optional modules in their MBA programme up to three years after your graduation to promote alumni's continuous development
mentor incoming students, to expand their network and enhance the relationship between academic and business.
*Offer of electives is subject to availability

learning: The Purposeful Leader module will include in its learning engagement an explicit opportunity for students to critically reflect about how they enact and embody purposeful/values-based leading and aspects of their organizational context which impacts on their ability to lead from this orientation;
There will be several opportunities, such as in Global Perspectives on Responsible Business, during which students will develop competencies in managing organisations responsibly.

The Managerial Finance module provides students the opportunities to explore the financial decision-making processes of organisations while working in groups to consider the several stakeholder and complexity of financial decisions.

The module Sustainable Operations will evaluate how operations management practices must respond to demands to address sustainability, including issued triggered by climate change and environmental concerns, the well-being of employees and communities.

Example is the module Understanding the Economy which will analyse how markets operate and evolve in view of the current green transitions, and what challenges in terms of production, costs, revenue, profit, and social value responsible businesses face within global value chains   to address environmental and social impacts.

Example is the Sustainable Operations module in which aspects such as product design and eco-design, adoption of environmental and social standards, amongst others are discussed with view on how they can contribute to drive business improvement.
